Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement in reply to questions asked by the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) and the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil). Imports of butter into Canada from the United Kingdom are not due as suggested by the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville, to the butter being "exported in transit," if by that the hon. member means shipped from an exporting country on an alternative bill-of-lading. Shipments of butter from exporting countries to the United Kingdom are not diverted to Canada while in transit.
In reply to that part of the hon. member's question as to whether imports from the United Kingdom are due to the fact that the United Kingdom is "producing more butter than they can consume." the answer is in the negative. The reason butter is imported from the United Kingdom is as follows. The tariff on butter entering Canada by direct shipment from New Zealand and Australia is, under the agreements with those dominions, 5 cents per pound while the British preferential rate of tariff applicable to shipments of butter from the United Kingdom is 8 cents per pmind. Six to eight weeks are required to secure delivery in Canada of butter on direct shipment from Australia or New Zealand and deliveries in Canada of butter from the United Kingdom may be secured in about ten days time. For this reason buying from the United Kingdom is less speculative and if imports of butter into Canada during the late winter or spring months are necessary, Canadian importers prefer to pay the higher rate of duty and import from the United Kingdom rather than to risk buying so far ahead as is necessary in order to secure the lower tariff rates on direct shipments from either New Zealand or Australia. Without reading it in full, I wish to refer to this part of the right hon. gentleman's remarks. Speaking on the 9th instant, the leader of the opposition stated:

lation which will prevent unfair practices and unethical proceedings on the part of the chairman of committees of this House of Commons when dealing with price spreads and mass buying, and on the part of some member or members of royal commissions when they are dealing with the same subjects.
In the first instance, I wish to point out that I was not chairman of the special committee of this house dealing with the matter of price spreads and mass buying. I was appointed chairman of the royal commission on price spreads on October 29 last, and throughout the deliberations of that commission I continued to act as chairman. The commissioners met on Tuesday morning last and signed their report at eleven o'clock. At four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon the report of the commissioners was handed by me to the Hon. Mr. Hanson, Minister of Trade and Commerce. Up to that time no authority was given by the commission as such, or in any way as a commission, for the release of any portion of that report or anything in respect to its deliberations. Following up the interrogations of the hon. member for Provencher may I ask i-f the commission will have power to deal with conditions such as those obtaining in the Red river area. The hon. member mentioned that some miles south of the city of Winnipeg this river formed the water supply for the people in that part of the province. However there is no possible chance in the wide world of the Red river forming a water supply for the people north of the city of Winnipeg, because from that city, on to lake Winnipeg, the river is simply a cesspool of sewage and infection. As a matter of fact just now -the Red river is not capable of carrying away the sewage from the city of Winnipeg. That is a very great menace. I was going to say it is a very obnoxious matter, but it is -more than that. The Red river of Manitoba has become a cesspool from the city of Winnipeg -to lake Winnipeg. Generally speaking I believe our whole country is drving out. At one time Manitoba was the site of a tremendous lake, but all that remains of that lake at present is a couple of comparatively small lakes, lake Winnipeg and lake Manitoba, and they are shrinking yearly. Hundreds of -thousands of acres of swamp land once covered with water are now as dry as the proverbial whistle. I believe it will be necessary for this federal government to deal not only with a limited portion of the country, as it is proposed at present, but that in the near future we will have to take into consideration this very serious situation in the province of Manitoba, to say nothing of the other western provinces. We will have to try to find some way to provide more moisture for the country.

I think this whole matter has been boiled down as well as it can be at present. It will be submitted to the advisory committee set up under this bill, and under that advisory committee there will be an executive committee. This work will be administered by the experimental farms branch under the Department of Agriculture, and they will have their own officials there to supervise it. In the illustration stations and farms-not the townships-the same principle will apply as has applied in the past to illustration stations. That is, men will receive certain remuneration for which they will agree to carry out certain work, and they will be supplied with seed. Previous to the introduction of this bill very careful consideration was given whether that should not also apply to all these farmers in the townships. It was

We have different types of contracts drawn up which will be considered when we go to western Canada. We feel that everything is in the best possible shape to expedite the work. speechtext:
First, with reference to the request made by the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly). On every occasion I have taken care not to paint too glowing a picture or give the impression that we hope to do what might be considered as the impossible thing. For example, as far as the building of dams and the planting of trees is concerned, no person is in a position to say that these things will have the tendency to produce rain. We hope to use the information we have in the best possible way and to go as far as we can to ensure greater economic security for the people in these districts should these climatic conditions oontinue, or, if for a time they do disappear, with greater rainfall, to prepare them to meet a similar condition should it recur; because, although the government of Canada and the provinces as well as the people have been very anxious to pour money into this great area, I am sure we all feel, whether we are outside the area or in it, that we cannot look forward, as has been suggested, to rain coming this year. So that should we have a number of bounteous years, and make no provision, should another dry period ensue, the only solution would be for the dominion to pour money again into the same area. As we have stated before, the fundamental thing we have in mind is to see whether, from the knowledge we have, supplemented and backed up by dominion finance, we can, give the farmers a very definite demonstration as to whether or not certain things will assist them, which they feel might be of advantage if they had the money, so as to enable them to go ahead. One of the difficulties with some of the farmers is this. For the first two or three years they achieved a fair success, but now their resources are so drained that they cannot do the things which they themselves believe would make them self sustaining.
The hon. member for Melville has said he sees nothing new in this. I believe his leader
said on one occasion this session that there is nothing new in the world, and with that statement I am inclined to agree in many respects. Those of us who know the people of western Canada agree that they do not want any great flare to be made about this. They want something substantial. They want us to go slowly, but they do want us to tackle these problems and to answer some of the questions that have been in their minds as to whether or not it is worth their while to remain in certain areas or to move out of the district. The only information we have is information obtained from other countries, and which we have collected. Where a man has not been successful through his own operations, to the extent that he should be, the reason has been that the districts around him have not followed the same cultural methods that he has.
As regards the observations of the hon. member for Willow Bunch, with respect to the question of water as compared with cultural methods, if we take steps that insure a water supply either for small communities or for larger communities, that will be one of the best things we can do to bring about greater economic security. I believe that about a thousand or more applications have been received for assistance in the building of small dams. The work might be done by the farmers themselves, but often the difference between success and failure, from the standpoint of the benefits derived from dams, depends on how the dam is put in, where it is, and on the engineering work in connection with it. As regards the labour, the people in the locality will themselves do the work-that is, apart from the engineering work. It is felt, in view of the difficulties in which they find themselves and the fact that their resources are depleted, that some assistance will have to be given these people in the way of material where necessary, and also in connection with the work they are doing.
As regards tree planting, there are two schools of thought. Some people hold that it is impossible to reap any benefit from the planting of trees in the wider shelter belts. They seem to think that it constitutes a trap for weeds, and others believe that they are killed out in the prolonged dry periods. We all agree however that we have in the west, both in the nursery station at Indian Head and in the substation at Saskatoon, men best qualified-and this is recognized not only in Canada but on the American continent-to give expert advice as to how far we can go in the planting of trees; and we shall be guided in that connection almost entirely by

The hon. member for Melville said that the Minister of Agriculture should be chairman of the advisory committee. That was also discussed in the drafting of the bill. It is under the administration of the minister, so that in that way he has full authority over the recommendations at least of this advisory committee. There is provision for two representatives from the federal Department of Agriculture. One of these is the director of the experimental farm system, because the actual work done here will be carried out under that branch of the department, and it is felt that he or the assistant director should be ex officio chairman, because meetings might be called at times when it would be difficult for the minister to be present. speechtext:
The minister assures us that there is nothing new in this bill, and is not in favour of making any spectacular estimate of what may be done under it. I agree with him, but he is a little late in making that pronouncement. This has already been heralded all over Canada as a great reclamation movement which will beneficially affect even the landscape and the climate. It has been talked about, written about and dreamed about, and I feel quite sympathetic with the minister in his intentions. But I am still further sympathetic with him that his friends should put him in wrong so much by making such extravagant prophecies as to what will be done. There is not a man in this house, familiar with that area, who does not know that the minister is undertaking a

tremendous task, and we believe the time has come when this effort should be made or that we should abandon that part of the country to wild life or give nature an opportunity to replace the grass and other [DOT] covering which was taken off by the husbandman, and which it may have taken millions of years to produce. The settlers took it off in about a quarter of a century and now, in a large part, it is a waste place. More than that, it is likely to damage areas further east and north of the worst affected area. I approve of the minister going at the problem, because the time has come when we must do something or get out, and I am not one who thinks that it should be the latter. This bill which is preceded by a resolution is, I suppose, a part of the reform policy of the government, but as already intimated it is merely an evolution of what has been under way for the last quarter of a century. It is true there is this brain trust, if I may call it so. That is what it is meant to be, and I hope it will be a brain trust with real practical brains. But there will be this difficulty. The minister is not on this committee but he will have to accept the responsibility for any action or inaction thereof; besides there is sure to be a difficulty in regard to getting decisions unless more local, practical farmers are appointed on it.
I believe in this policy of rehabilitation, and I want to say a friendly word with respect to every feature of the bill if I can do so conscientiously.
Prior to last June, I do not think the word "rehabilitation" was in the government's vocabulary as applied to this area, neither has it been in former years. But we have never before had such a scourge as we have had during the last five or six years. In former years, only one or two years and sometimes only one would be dry at a time, and the following year there would be double the crop. For instance, 1914 was one of the very worst' years we had in that area and indeed over much of northern and eastern Saskatchewan, but it was followed in 1915 by the most remarkable crop we have ever seen. When that happens, we forget all about the former bad years. Now we have had six dry years in succession and the minister has at last broken new ground by bringing down a bill to provide for an advisory committee. I approve the name of the bill; I believe in having an advisory committee on this matter, but I would like to see on it more practical farmers from the area concerned, men who must know a great deal more about the problem than anybody else.

______________Rehabilitation oj Drought Areas
In addition to that, there is a sum of money to be associated with the scheme, and that is good too, but all that, with the exception of the committee, was available before. However, this is really a start and to that extent we would commend the minister. But he speaks of the length of time the government have been preparing for this and the data they have secured. Well, if they had the data and if the seasons have been growing worse instead of better, why did they not start in 1931? I remember hearing the Prime Minister on the first day of June, 1931, announcing from his seat in the house that a national calamity had stricken the southern prairies of the western provinces and everybody was visibly impressed by his statement that this was a national calamity. Why has the government not acted nationally prior to this year? In a couple of months or so, by next July, four years will have elapsed since that statement was made, and it is left until now for the government, recognizing the national nature of this problem, to take steps by bringing down this meagre bill. This is the result of four years' cogitation. I must confess I feel disappointed. I was, I suppose, infected with the same virus or bacteria or whatever you choose to call it that other enthusiasts were affected with who read the glowing description in the Toronto paper to which I referred on a former occasion, stating that the minister was to take this area under his wing as a sort of little crown colony affair and was going to do wonders. Those papers did the minister an injustice; we all know he cannot do that. All we can do is to do our best and leave nothing undone that is within our power in the way of expenditure or the appointment of this committee to advise or any other committee or individual that would like to tender advice.
1 would like to make this suggestion at this stage; I am afraid the minister has started off on the wrong foot. I remember quite distinctly that the premier of Manitoba got busy early in connection with this proposition, more than a year ago, and I should like to have seen the minister show a little stronger disposition to cooperate with the provinces. Of course he tells us that he is cooperating, but we would like to see some more practice of that nature and some more evidence of cooperation than merely a pious wish to cooperate. As a matter of fact the minister is invading what is strictly provincial work. It is true that in a small way, in an experimental, demonstration way, the dominion was in it before and was recognized as being within its jurisdiction. But now, to go into an area of that proportion without the closest consultation with the three provinces concerned,
I think is undiplomatic. Questions regarding production are essentially provincial in character. There is no law delineating where provincial powers and activities in agriculture stop and those of the dominion begin, but over a period of many years there has grown up between the dominion and provincial departments of agriculture a practice that allocates questions of production to the provinces. This is invading that field to greater extent than has been the case previously that I think the first thing to do, if I might so suggest, would be for the Minister of Agriculture to call the provinces together, take counsel with them and say: Here, I want to help you further than I have done in the past, to aid you in such a way that we shall have some business intercourse with the rural municipalities; in order to do that we must have your assistance. The municipalities are of course the creation of the province, and I do not see how in the world much is going to be accomplished if such a course is not taken. For instance, there is the establishment of grazing areas. In my estimation one of the first things that should be done in that area is to segregate as much as possible those lighter lands that are more predisposed to drift and on which nothing can be grown in a dry year. Lands with lighter subsoil and of a gravelly nature, that are hit worse in a dry year, should be seeded down as rapidly as possible. How is the federal government going to acquire those lands without invading provincial rights? I do not want to raise that difficulty, but it is there just the same. Many of those lands are reverting to the municipalities or the provinces now for taxes; how can the dominion government handle them unless they have the cooperation and very close cooperation of the provinces? Unless these matters are attended to at the outset, we shall have three provincial governments, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, each running little shows of their own, and on top of that the federal government running theirs; that is what it will mean. I cannot help thinking the dominion is now taking a step in the direction of invading provincial aedtivities in the matter of production to an extent that it did not do before, and yet not to a sufficient extent to be of any use except as a natural evolution of what has been taking place in the past. Therefore, unless we get those areas seeded down as quickly as possible and thereby make those dust storms, subside-because not only is damage caused to the area from which the dust blows, but also to the area on to which the dust is blown,-our little activities as described in this bill will never be noticed;
2636	COMMONS
Rehabilitation of Drought Areas
the dust will blow faster than the remedy can overtake it.
We do not need to go to Arabia or the Sahara desert to see what happens; all we have to do is to' look across the United States boundary and see right in the panhandle of Texas, Nebraska, Colorado, Oklahoma and a number of adjoining states, the terrific storms of dust occurring now as we talk taking not only the top soil, but the subsoil in some places to a depth of two or three feet. That is what is happening to the south of us and that is what will happen in our country unless effective measures are taken right away. The point is this: will this legislation bring about the desired result? It is good as far as it goes, but I am afraid you will never see it in the midst of one of these storms that are liable to occur any day in that territory, as has occurred in a relatively small way even this spring. I suppose there has to be a beginning with all things, but one should at least start diplomatically, start with a feeling that everyone interested is backing you, and particularly the provincial governments, who are all actively concerned about this problem and have their plans already worked out. It may be that the minister has conferred with them, but not as far as I know. Such conference it seems to me should have preceded any action. For instance, do the provinces know about this bill? Were they consulted about it? What is their opinion about it?
I have nothing further to add except to congratulate the minister on breaking new ground, introducing a new term in relation to this area so far as the government is concerned, the word "rehabilitation." But I trust they will back it up by something more substantial in the way of remedial measures than are provided for in this bill.

All their information and service will be available. We called a meeting some time ago in Ottawa at which some of the prime movers of that committee were present. The whole point is that as I said, we do not want this committee to become unwieldy.

One difficulty is to obtain a supply of suitable seed. That is what I had in mind when I made the statement on this in connection with my estimates, that we believe it is absolutely essential to get a sufficient quantity of seed so that we can almost afford to waste it in giving it away, once we have demonstrated beyond doubt where it should be used to the best advantage. We have practical control of all the best seed that we think suitable, at least of sufficient of it for our needs, and it has been put out where it will grow and multiply most rapidly and it will still be kept under control with the aim of having within another year from half to three quarters of a million pounds of the best kind available, together with much larger quantities of seed clover and brome grass, though perhaps not so much of the most hopeful strain of brome grass.

I realize that strictly speaking we are not considering means of dealing with the drought menace in the west, but a bill for the appointment of a commission to act in the matter. However, there are one or two points which I think should
be mentioned here and now. For the last fifty years m Manitoba we have been doing our best to drain off the water. The province is furrowed with deep ditches. We have a fairly ample and abundant supply of water in the spring, but soon after the freshets set in the water is gone. I realize that this is a provincial matter but it seems to me that if the province would take means to block a number of these ditches it would have a very beneficial effect.
There is another matter. There are, or there were a few years ago, hundreds of flowing wells, actually hundreds in the vicinity of Winnipeg. There are a great number of dairy men and milk producers in that vicinity and none were satisfied Unless they got running water. They bored wells some of which were hundreds of feet deep. The water is running away, and no doubt that fact is having a very unfavourable effect so far as the moisture condition is concerned. The point which is causing me the greatest annoyance is that mentioned only a few moments ago by the minister, namely the circumstances in connection with tree planting. Just as in the past fifty years we have been doing our best to run the water off, we are now doing our best to cut down all the trees in the province. At one time the city of Winnipeg used to be heated in the winter time by coal. That was a proper procedure

and may I say right here that I have neither coal nor wood interests. However because wood has been cheaper during the past few years thousands of cords of it have been brought to Winnipeg to heat the city during the winter months. Although it is brought from low-lying districts of the province, we have no assurance that in the future those districts will not be as dry as other districts now are. Certainly we have no assurance that the trees will grow again. I realize that this is not a matter with which the minister may be able to deal, but I hope what I have said may reach the ears of members of the government in Manitoba. I do not know whether or not they have ever considered the fact that they are cutting down all the trees in the province, and that if they continue the time may soon come when we shall have none left. I sincerely trust my observations may reach them, and it is for that reason I have risen to speak.

Could we not have more local farmers on the advisory committee? I am not taking exception to any who are on as provided in the bill; I think probably the classification has been well made, but may I point out to the minister that the live stock men on the committee would almost surely counteract the grain farmers' influence by way of reclamation. If one were to ask the average rancher what he thinks he would probably tell you this area should never have been opened for homesteading at all-none of it. Inasmuch as we cannot revert to the time thirty years ago when it was all ranch property, we have to deal with it as it is. I was wondering if the minister had gained any information from his experts, a number of whom are well posted on this area, and if they believe it would be better to let nature take charge of these lighter land areas composed of soils which tend to drift and which except in good years, cannot produce crops. Would it not become covered by whatever verdure nature may supply, such as Russian thistles, cacti, sage brush or any other plant indigenous to dry areas? Then through time grasses would appear. Nobody knows where they come from, but the fact is they do come. We know the birds distribute seeds, and other seeds are blown in from neighbouring districts. There is an area between Medicine Hat and Brooks about eighty miles in length which at one time was under cultivation and which now has a first class sod, affording good pasture just by letting it alone. Of course the longer the land has been under cultivation, the slower will be the process of regrassing carried on by nature. It seems to me anything would be better than repeatedly stirring up these light soils and allowing them to be blown away. Not only are those particular places injured, but the drifting soil causes injury where it may light as already pointed out.

If there were a few more dirt farmers on the committee I believe the results would be more satisfactory. They are the men who know the country and have been struggling against odds to try .to make it go in the tilling of the safer wheat areas. Their advice would be valuable in ascertaining what would be best to do, and whether it would be wise to attempt to seed artificially by means of domestic grasses .or to let nature do the seeding with anything it wishes to produce, in order that the nakedness of old mother earth might be covered up. I must repeat my belief that even at the risk of it being a little unwieldy there should be more dirt farmers on the committee.

speechtext:
With reference to the first point raised by the hon. member for Melville, may I say we have the information of ranchers and farmers, as well as officials of the department, to the effect that we can give great assistance and can speed up to a considerable extent the reclamation of this land to a point where it may be suitable for pasture and ranch property. The Tilley area to which the hon. member referred, was used for a great many years, was then abandoned and is now covered by grasses. The type of grass which seems to have made the most rapid gain is the sand grass, which is really the natural grass found on very light land. I agree entirely with what the hon. member has said about .the cultivation of land which was too light to give much promise of a continuation of heavy crops, about the working out of the fibre which was in it, and bringing the soil to a point where it greatly resembled a desert.
The purpose of the undertaking is simply to investigate, to demonstrate what can be done .and the best way in which it can be done. However the .actual physical setting aside of certain areas for either ranching or farming is the prerogative of the province. The information which we obtain will be made available to the provinces. Perhaps it is not quite fair to make1 that statement, because the committees in each of these provinces have for years been working together. The experimental farm officials are not the only ones who have been gathering information. The federal representative sits in with the provincial representatives, and those from the various universities in western Canada. Once a year at the meeting of the national advisory committee on agricultural services we have a joint meeting at which all the work is re-

subsubtopic: WORK FOR RECLAMATION OF DRIED OUT LANDS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext: I think the minister touched on a very important matter when he said the responsibility of setting aside these badly drifted areas and devoting them to grass and community pastures is really a prerogative of the province. In making that statement he indicated that the most important thing that should be done immediately is a provincial duty, if I understood him aright. Therefore I was wondering if the minister would consider the advisability of assisting the province financially in converting these areas into community pastures in order to have the drifting stopped as quickly as possible. That would be in addition to the other activities that are provided for and which have been more or less under evolution and trial for twenty-five years. I do not think there is enough grass seed in Canada to seed the areas that should be closed out as quickly as possible.

That is a provincial duty, and it seems to me that would be a great step forward to leave this to the province but assist them financially in doing so. Of course this advisory committee will have to be consulted. They will know more about the local details than I do, because I have not been in that area for some time and I would not care to prescribe in particulars. At the same time I know there are areas where you cannot grow grain and other areas where you can. We want to salvage and rescue the good areas and convert the others into something more useful than sources of drifting sand. Would the minister consult the Minister of Finance and his other
colleagues in regard to doing something financially to take care of these prospective pasture areas with which the province has the primary duty, as he indicated?

speechtext: We have been doing, and under this scheme it is intended to do, just exactly what the hon. member has suggested. Realizing the importance of having almost unlimited supplies of these grass and clover seeds in connection with this work, we have made a survey as to where they can be multiplied most rapidly. We have practically taken control of sufficient of the best of the seed that is available to ensure this supply in the shortest time possible. I think there is no necessity of dwelling longer on this fact, that this is really part of the project. Next year we may require a larger vote in this connection to adopt whatever means may be necessary to multiply a larger quantity of grass seeds that we will keep on hand. It is intended that this grass seed shall be made available as soon as sufficient quantities have been multiplied, and of all the grasses of which there are sufficient quantities, as soon as we have discovered the best possible use to make of it.

At the present time we are in the fog. In the past five years, at least fifty times, I have insisted on the importance of classifying the unemployed according to trade or profession. Last year the Prime Minister agreed that it was a very sensible suggestion and finally this year the suggestion has met with the approval of the Minister of Labour. I have taken advantage of the visit of the mayors to Ottawa to ask
these sixty-eight municipalities to give me the information asked for. It will be very representative of the unemployment problem throughout Canada, because the capital city of each province was represented in that delegation; and if we have those figures we shall know the number of unemployed who are employable, according to trade or profession, in the larger cities of the country. It is for that reason that I have taken a few minutes to mention these facts to the committee. I maintain that it will be impossible for the government to draft any constructive policy with regard to the relief of unemployment until the unemployed are so classified. Each one must be considered individually, just as the soldiers were looked after individually when they were wounded on the battlefield. It is the only way to deal with the problem, and I hope that if some of the municipalities already referred to were reluctant to give the information asked for, some means should be taken, either by this government or by the provincial governments, or by federal and provincial governments together, if there is an interprovincial conference, to see that the information is secured. That information, as soon as it is secured, and if compiled by the bureau of statistics, would give the government an opportunity to draft a policy which might be of duration for the relief of the unemployed.

It is quite true that in the Public Works Construction Act of last year reference is made to tenders being asked for before a contract is awarded by governor in council, but I claim that the general law should apply. The hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) criticized this matter last year and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) made the following statement, to be found on page 4422 of Hansard:
But although it is not provided that public tenders must be called for it does not follow that they will not be. The principle has not been abandoned. These works have to be carried out under the direction of the governor in council, and assigned to the particular department and the minister which may appear to be best equipped to carry them on. Already, in anticipation of the passing of this bill, a large number of advertisements have been published by the Public Works Department calling for tenders, and there is no reason to assume that the government is abandoning the well established and sound principle of inviting public tenders. I can assure my hon. friend that the government are as sensible of their responsibility in this matter as any member of the opposition can be.
I protest against the new system introduced by the Minister of Marine for the granting of such important contracts. He is doing away with the safeguard of calling for public tenders.

So far as any works to be carried out under his jurisdiction are concerned, does the minister intend to encourage only his own friends to tender? I am not criticizing the policy at the moment, I simply want to know what the minister intends to do.
What did you do?
When the Liberals were in power it was public tenders all the time.

An inquiry was made some time ago on this same matter and I said, no. I think this answer is confirmed by the list I have just given to the committee. I will state quite frankly that I was advised by the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) but I have been told that there are firms on this list known as Liberal firms.
Which ones?
I do not know them all but I will mention the Morton company.
Are they Liberals?
Who told you they were Liberals?

If my hon. friend were told the names of those interested in this company, I think he would agree that the majority of them are Liberals. I do not want to discuss this point further at the moment. However, I would say to my hon. friends from Quebec that the Liberal administration of that province has carried on a certain custom for a number of years. If I understood the statements made by the, hon. member for Quebec East some time ago in the city of Quebe-c, the hon. member is a great friend of and even responsible for the Liberal administration of Quebec. He stated that there was only one Liberal party in all the provinces of Canada. He stated there was solidarity between the Liberal administration in Quebec and the Liberal members of this house. He stated there was the same solidarity as far as the Liberal administration of Ontario is concerned. My hon. friend wanted to know why tenders had not been asked for from the firm of A. Deslauriers Limited. I will ask my hon. friend- to get the information from his friends of the Quebec government and tell this committee what amount of money has been paid to this firm during the last fifteen years by the Quebec administration. When I was a member of the Quebec legislature I can remember the public buildings which were built by this company. In many instances no tenders were called for by the Taschereau government; at times the work was awarded simply by verbal contract. Hundreds of thousands of dollars have been paid to this company by that administration. My hon. friends say that we were not justified in withholding opportunities to bid from other contractors, but I contend that the public interest was safeguarded as a large number of firms were called to tender. I do not think the hon. member for Quebec East was serious when he asked me to call for tenders from the different firms mentioned in his letter. Tenders were called for from ten firms which I understood were reliable, and- the contract was awarded to the lowest tenderer. The amount involved, $356,000, was a very low price. I ask the hon. member to get from his friends in the Department of Public Works at Quebec a list of the public works which were undertaken during the last five years, a list of the firms who were asked to tender, the contractors who secured the contract and the subcontracts, the amounts paid to all these contractors and subcontractors, and-1 think my hon. friend will easily learn, what I am stating to this committee, that the custom was established by the Liberal administration and approved by my hon. friend from Quebec East -entirely approved. I have never heard a

Supply-Public Works
word either from my 'hon. friend from Quebec East or from the hon. member for Quebec South as to the methods employed by the Liberal administration of Quebec in asking for tenders for public works; and we have thought it advisable to give some encouragement to other reliable firms in Quebec, provided the public interest is safeguarded.

I am not quite sure that
what the minister has said justifies this government in not following the practice which the Minister of Public Works himself has considered to be a sound one, namely, calling for public tenders. I do not know that all the bad example which might have been given by the government of the province of Quebec would justify the Minister of Marine in the contention which he now makes that this Public Works Construction Act is for the purpose of encouraging his friends. I thought it was to provide relief.
I never said that, sir.

I understood the minister
to say-I think I heard him rightly-that for the past five years in the province of Quebec contracts have been let in the manner in which this present contract has been.

The last fifteen or
twenty years.

At any rate, for the last
five years. Am I right in saying that the minister stated that for the past five years that has been the method?

Perhaps fifteen or
twenty years.

I took the trouble at six
o'clock to call up the Minister of Public Works of Quebec, the Hon. Mr. Francoeur, and asked him to allow me to state on his behalf what was the policy and procedure followed in awarding contracts for public buildings in the public works department of Quebec, and he told me that with one exception, the details of which he could not give at the moment, all public buildings erected since he became minister, in 1930 or 1931. had been erected after tenders had been called for publicly in the newspapers of the province. I have no reason to doubt his word, and if the Minister of Marine has any reason for doubting it I have no doubt the Hon. Mr. Francoeur will write him. Mr. Francoeur stated that in connection with the most recent public building for which a contract was let in the city of Quebec, the extension to the parliament buildings, public tenders were called for, and the same with the Quebec gaol, a building constructed in recent years-
Hear, hear.

Oh, there is no chance for
the minister or any of his friends to get in; it is a women's gaol and we are careful. That was built after public tenders had been called for. In connection with the extension to the parliament buildings on St. Augustine street, public tenders were called for in the newspapers, and he mentioned two or three others. He said he had not the facts of every case before him but he could authorize me to say that with one exception tenders were called for in the newspapers. That was a good example to follow. I would suggest that the minister instead of following the bad old example of fifteen years ago, with reforming which he no doubt had a lot to do when he was a member of the Quebec legislature -instead of following that bad old system I suggest that if he would follow the good, modern, up to date system which is in effect in Quebec we would all agree, and both he and I would support that government in Quebec which he blames us for supporting at the moment.
But I have a little grievance of my own against the minister. Away back in February some time I asked for a return of all orders in council passed under the Public Works Construction Act by the Department of Marine. I had also asked for orders in council passed by the Department of Public Works, and the Minister of Public Works, who had far more business to do, was kind and courteous enough to produce a large file of them-they spread all over these desks.
Too big.

As a matter of fact the
ex-Minister of Public Works has not slept nights for looking through this file. The Minister of National Defence also produced orders in council and the Minister of the Interior produced some. But of all those that were carried out by the Department of Marine we have five, whereas I think I have a list of some twenty-five orders in council that were passed in connection with these public works. I am well aware that the minister will say to me that under the act he is not obliged to do anything more than publish a precis of these orders in council in the Canada Gazette if they were passed when the house was not sitting, and that he must produce them forthwith if the house
Supply-Public Works

is sitting. That is the proper interpretation of the act, I believe. But I call his attention to the fact that I asked him for the production of these orders in council and he has delayed for a period of well over six weeks. The minister had all these orders in council, a number of which were passed as far back as August-for instance, the painting of the harbour bridge was passed in August, and the Quebec transit sheds in November. That was the second order in council.

Did my hon. friend
ask by letter?

No, it was a return of the
house, a long time ago.
A motion for the production of papers?

Yes. I asked for all orders under the Public Works Construction Act, and I think I asked specifically in connection with the Marine department. I asked for all orders in council passed under the Public Works Construction Act. But not only that; I have been in communication with the minister's department for the past week or so, asking that they be hustled. I did not want to rise on the orders of the day as a matter of privilege; I know the minister does not like that and I do not like it either. But it would have been only fair to have these orders in council ready for the time we were to have a discussion on these matters. I do not want to make individious comparisons, but the Minister of Public Works has presented all his orders passed prior to the opening of the session, and as soon as any other order in council is passed while the house is in session it is produced. He is producing them every day and the orders in council in the Public Works department must run into the hundreds.
Mr. E'LLIOTT: He is passing far too many.

As a matter of fact he is
passing far too many for our convenience. I will ask the Minister of Marine to produce the following orders:
Also one about Whitehead, the number of which the minister forgot, but it is dated October 25.
And will he explain how it is that order was passed on January 14, 1935.

Also, if he will be so kind, will he produce the correspondence and in particular the tenders filed with the department at both the first call and the second call for tenders in the case of the Quebec transit sheds, the item which we are now discussing, marked in the appropriations of last year as $463,000? We would be glad if the minister would produce these before we have any further discussion of this matter some other evening.

Would it also be possible for the minister to bring down the correspondence with regard to the first tenders that were asked for and before the granting of the contract, that is -the correspondence exchanged between my hon. friend and various firms of Quebec city and I understand there is some correspondence from some of his colleagues. Of course there is nothing personal in that, and it would be very helpful in the discussion of this matter.

Answering the hon.
member for Quebec South, I have no objection whatever to filing not only the orders in council mentioned by my hon. friend, but all (the orders in council passed under the Public Works Construction Act. I think -the motion of my hon. friend did not mention the Department of Marine, because it was not brought to the attention of my officials. I am quite sure if that motion had been brought to their attention, all the orders in council would have been filed right away. As soon as they are certified, I will file copies of all the orders in council.
Will the minister also inquire from the officials whether they are aware of the fact that an order for a return was passed by this house long ago?

I remember a few days ago my assistant deputy minister discussed the matter with me and spoke about the meaning of that section of the legislation about filing all those orders in council. He was not sure whether we were bound to file all -the orders in council or only those passed under general items of the schedule.

I do not want to give the minister a lesson in constitutional law, but

Supply-Public Works
he ought to know that if there is an order of the house calling for filing all the orders in council, it does not matter what the act says; he has to file them.
I understand that, but the hon. member's motion was not brought to the attention of my officials or I would have complied immediately with the order.
When an order of the house is passed calling for the tabling of certain orders in council, it is not necessary to discuss the interpretation of a statute with the officials of the department.

That is what I am saying to my hon. friend. Probably my officials were not aware of that order, because they came to me and discussed the interpretation of the act. Had they known1 of that order, they would not have discussed that interpretation; they would have tabled the orders in council. They will be tabled anyway within a day or two.
As regards what the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) has said about the Cummins Construction Company Limited of Montebello, that firm did not file any tender, so that it does not matter whether they were asked to tender or not.
There must be some good contracting firms in Timbuctoo from whom the minister might call for tenders the next time, and then he would have a very respectable list.
Could my hon. friend bring down the correspondence?
I shall be pleased to .bring down everything we have in connection with those works.
That would be better than discussing the deeds or misdeeds of the Taschere.au government.
The statement of the Minister of Marine is not finished yet.
What is the number of the order in council?
It is No. 844. I might give immediately an explanation of the reason why the contract has been awarded to a Montreal firm. This is a very special work.
Oh, oh.
The hon. member for Quebec East may laugh-
That seems to be all I can do.

-my hon. friend may know more than the engineers in that respect. I will bring down the correspondence if my hon. friend wants it. I will show him a report from the engineers that only three firms can do that work properly, namely: Concrete Repairs Limited; Gunite and Waterproofing Company, and Western Waterproofing Company Limited, Montreal.

What engineer gave
advice?
Consulting engineer Ernest Gohier of Montreal. He is an outstanding engineer.
His picture was in the paper.
I do not know that, but he is a first class engineer and his report was to that effect.
When was the order in council passed?
On April 2, 1935.
Has it been tabled and, if not, why not?
It will be tabled with the others.
It is all very well to lie down on the job of tabling those passed before the session, but those passed during the session must be tabled forthwith. That is the law.
It might have been tabled; I am not sure.

The minister said it was not. It is not my job to teach the minister the law; he ought to know what the law is. I would call his attention to the fact that he has to observe some rules; peace, order and good government must be observed here. I think this is a terrible thing.
That was passed only on April 2.
It has not been tabled. Next one?
Saint John, NJ3.
Are there no more in Quebec?
No more in Quebec.

What about the $730,000?
Supply-Public Works
No tenders are asked for yet.

It is marked "contract" here in the report given by the Minister of Finance, statement of moneys expended under the authority of the Public Works Construction Act, 1934, chapter 59 of the statutes of 1934, in the fiscal year 1934-35 up to February 28, 1935. Amongst other things it says: "Quebec, new quay wall to widen pier No. 1, west side, $730,000," and under "contract or day labour," it says, "contract." Expenditure $1000; commitments outstanding $14,000. Now what is that all about?
I am sure that the plans and specifications were in only lately, and no tenders have been asked for yet. Probably there was some preparatory work done by the harbour commission.

Apart from admonishing the minister to keep the house advised, he ought to keep his colleague the Minister of Finance advised as to what he is doing, because I am sure the Minister of Finance does not want to deceive the house, and he has it here in his statement.
Next?
Saint John, N.B., item 153, $2,000,000. work not started yet, and no tenders asked for yet. There are works of demolition which have been done last year and not completed yet, done by day labour.

Again the statement of the Minister of Finance filed in the house shows expenditure and outstanding commitments from inception to February 28, 1935, Saint John. N.B.. reconstruction of berths 1, 2, 3 and 4, $2,000,000. Is that the item to which the minister refers? Under the heading "contract or day labour" it says "cost plus contract"; under the heading, "expenditure," $119.967.61; under the heading, "commitments outstanding," $155,032.39. That seems a lot of money.
These are demolition works which have been awarded to a firm in Saint John at cost plus.
It is a pretty nifty little contract, $155,000.
These works are done by day labour by the Saint John Dry dock Company Limited.
But it is all under this $2,000,000. Was it a contract?

There was a contract given to the Saint John Drydock Company Limited for the demolition of the old pier at cost plus. But as to the reconstruction, no contracts have been awarded yet and no tenders asked for.
Is the minister in a position to tell us who was the contractor?
Yes, I have just stated, Saint John Drydock Company Limited under an order in council.
What is the percentage on the demolition contract?
I think it is four per cent, I am not sure. I shall have the order in council at the next sitting and give the information to my hon. friend.
Were any tenders called for the demolition of these piers and works?
No, I do not think so. It was given "cost plus" because we considered that the Saint John Drydock Company was the best firm in Saint John to do the work. Also they are good Grits.
That is the reason they get four per cent.

I am not concerned with that aspect of the question; I am more concerned about the cost and the saving that could be made. I would like to know why no tenders were called for that kind of work. It is a very substantial amount. So far about $300,000 is involved and we do not know whether this will complete the work of demolishing these structures; it may amount to half a million or a million. We should know why no tenders were called for that large amount of work. I think the law provides for the calling of tenders for works above a certain amount.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, April 12, 1935
The house- met at three o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, may I make an explanation to the house with refer-

Price Spreads Commission
ence to remarks I made yesterday in referring to the price spreads report? I referred to having compared what appeared in the press with what was in the report and stated that there was evidence that whoever had "given the report to the press had had an intimate association with it. I had not known at the time that the report had not been tabled. The comparison that I had made was between what appeared in the press on Monday night and a fuller account which appeared on a subsequent day in the press elsewhere, and which spoke of matters following as "major points contained in the report."
I assumed that when the report had been signed and presented to the minister it had been immediately tabled and that what I was reading in the press was from what the minister himself had tabled. I need not say that I have not seen the report itself, and in fact it was not until after I had spoken that I discovered that the report had not been tabled.

subtopic: PUBLICATION OF REPORT IN THE PRESS IN ADVANCE OF PRESENTATION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I was not in the house when the right hon. leader of the opposition brought to the attention of the house the .matter which he described as of very grave importance to the liberties and dignities of the House of Commons. I am not going into any great discussion of that phase of the matter.
The right hon. gentleman made two statements to the house. His first statement was made on Tuesday and I propose not to deal with that, statement to-day. In that statement the right hon. gentleman by innuendo reflected upon myself, but I shall deal with that amply and fully at a future time.
Yesterday the right hon. gentleman raised again the question to which he has now just referred; that is, the publication in the press of Monday of what was undoubtedly a summary of the findings of the commission. I have listened with some interest to the explanation which the right hon. gentleman gives of what is recorded in Hansard of yesterday. I shall not seek to follow that method of explanation. What I shall say will be very direct and very definite and will leave no doubt in anyone's mind as to the accuracy of my statement.
In the first place before I make this statement I draw the attention of the house to several somewhat singular things, and the first is this, that there has been a singular excitement about one particular disclosure. The second is this, that during the past six weeks there have been continuous leaks from the commission, responsibility for which I absolutely and unreservedly disclaim. Personally
I was not much concerned about it. I knew, as hon. members sitting within my hearing now know, that much of the deliberations of the commission were necessarily and properly discussed with those not members of the commission. But I was curious as I read the Hansard report of yesterday to know why no reference was made to the publication on Friday last of almost the full verbatim minority report; and why no question was raised as to the publication last week of a fairly complete summary; and why no question was raised as to the publication of a summary nearly two weeks ago and as to many other incidents of leakage for which I state without reserve I accept no responsibility.
As regards the summary to which the right hon. gentleman has drawn attention and in reference to which he himself said yesterday, and explains it away to-day, that he had .compared it with the report, I have this to say: I was as much surprised as any hon. member of the house when I learned of the publication of this information on Monday last, nor did I know until to-day how it had reached the press. However, I find that I must take the responsibility for this information having reached the hands of the press. No one regrets more than I do its premature publication.
I have one further word to say. Yesterday one hon. gentleman interjected into the Lilliputian discussion a reference or insinuation that there had been a violation of an oath of office. I think I owe it to myself and others to quote the oath of the commissioners which was as follows:
You do solemnly and sincerely promise and swear that you will duly and faithfully and to to the best of your skill and knowledge execute and perform the office of commissioner under part I of the Inquiries Act and upon the authority of order in council No. 1461 of the 7th of July, 1934, to continue, complete and report upon the investigation of the select special committee of the House of Commons in the question of the spread of prices for commodities.
There is no reference in part I of the Inquiries Act to the release of information. I am not attempting to justify anything on that score but I want to remove any doubt from the mind of anyone who may have heard the suggestion that there was a violation of an oath of office by any member of the commission who may have disclosed what went on. I notice also that in answering the roll call yesterday several .members of the commission did not in any sense disclaim responsibility. One asked for a commission, another endorsed his observation, a third did likewise while others made statements regarding the
Price Spreads Commission

release of information. I repeat that as far as I am concerned I regret the premature publication of this summary and while I take full responsibility for it, I do so with the knowledge and a clear conscience that there was no intention of violating any confidence.

Mr. Speaker, the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) has just dealt with my remarks of yesterday in relation to the report of the royal commission. He said he would deal later with what he regarded as a reflection upon himself as chairman of the committee which had to do with the price spreads investigation. May I say to him that the ground upon which I based my remarks in that connection was the correspondence tabled in this house some .time ago, and which contained a communication dated October 26, 1934, from the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to the hon. gentleman in which the following paragraph appears:
It is fundamentally unsound that the chairman of a select committee and of a royal commission, whether or not a member of the government, should publicly discuss the committee's proceedings before the evidence had been completed' and a report thereon made by the royal commission, especially in view of the rule that prevents members of the House of Commons from discussing in the house proceedings before its committees until final report has been made. Conclusions or judgments should not be pronounced until taking of evidence is completed and arguments heard thereon.
That is the correspondence upon which my remark was based. I had also as authority what is known to every hon. member of the house as to the extent to which my hon. friend would be violating the rules in publishing proceedings before a committee before any report thereon had been made to the house.

Mr. Speaker, I spoke to a question of privilege but I do not know what the right hon. gentleman has spoken to. I hope the house will indulge me while I make a brief further statement. I had no desire to go into the discussion of Tuesday last but the right hon. gentleman has made necessary a further reply. As a member of twenty-four years' standing in this house, I claim the liberty of replying. On Tuesday last the right hon. gentleman said:
I should like to suggest also that when the government are considering the legislation that is to be based upon the recommendations of this commission, with respect to unfair practices and unethical proceedings, it might consider whether it is not possible to enact some legislation _ which will prevent unfair practices and unethical proceedings on the part of the chairmen of committees of this House of
[Mr. Stevens.J
Commons when dealing with price spreads and mass buying.
The right hon. gentleman made no specific reference to myself but as I was the only chairrfian of a price spreads and mass buying committee of this house the suggestion or innuendo is that I was unfair as chairman and unethical in my practices in connection with the discharge of that duty. Outside of the house the right hon. gentleman has described me as a hypocrite because of my attitude and the speeches I delivered in connection with this matter.
At the outset I must say that I have no apology to offer to the right hon. gentleman or to any other man, firm or group in this country as to my attitude on this subject. I should like to ask this question: To whom have I been unfair? I think the answer is clear, and I should like to review it. I was charged with being unfair while chairman of the commission to Mr. Stanley McLean, president of the Canada Packers Limited. I have been charged with being unfair to Sir Joseph Flavelle and the Robert Simpson Company. I have been charged with being unfair to the T. Eaton Company. I have been charged with being unfair to the tobacco industry and the National Fish Company as well as to some others. 'Charges have been made that I was prejudiced and unfair to these people and to these concerns.
I now ask this question: Has anyone during the last fifteen months, five of which I was chairman of the committee and*subsequently a private member of the commission, charged me with being unfair to the workers, to the farmers, to the growers of vegetables and fruits, to the small merchants from one end of Canada to the other or to the cattlemen who appeared before that committee? If anybody is prepared to point out a single instance where I failed to give fair treatment to him, then I should be alarmed and ready to make amends. 'But these, sir, are not my accusers. The accuser, in regard to the quotation from some of the correspondence read by the right hon. gentleman a moment ago, was Mr. Burton of The Robert Simpson Company. He was the accuser; he is the gentleman whom the right hon. gentleman cites to-day as being-

He is the one whom the right hon. gentleman cites to-day in giving grounds for my unfairness. No other person made any accusation at that time in regard to the correspondence to which the right hon. gentleman alluded.
And now I turn to the correspondence, which referred to the pamphlet that was issued last July. I have kept pretty silent about this matter. I have not up to the present resented or explained or answered accusations in regard to the issue of that so-called pamphlet. I shall do so now as clearly as I can, and I venture to say there sit in this house fifty members who can verify the accuracy of my statement.
There is in this parliament a club known as the study club, under the chairmanship of a distinguished member of this house. It consists solely of members of parliament and I think the object of the club is a good one. I have had the honour of addressing it on two or more occasions. On the occasion in question, it was at the end of the last session. I am not quite certain whether the price spreads committee had completed its work, but it was within a day or so of the end of the session. I was asked to address them on the subject and to analyze and summarize the work of the committee. I saw nothing that was wrong in doing that, and I did it and did it very frankly. It has been the practice of that club to have a reporter present who takes down the speech of whoever happens to be the guest speaker. This was done, not at my request; it was done and later the report was submitted to me. There sit in this house a number of hon. gentlemen who urged me to furnish them with a number of copies of that speech. I intimated that I did not care to have the speech published as it was delivered extemporaneously. However, I corrected the copy and it was mimeographed at my own expense. I did not circulate it. It has never been circulated yet as far as I know, and in so far as the mimeograph to which I refer is concerned, with the exception of a certain number of copies that were sent to a few representative press men in this country, in confidence, and not by myself. The speech got into the press subsequently.
I have no apologies to make for anything that was in that speech-none whatever. The speech was accurate in the main. When it appeared however Mr. Burton of the Robert Simpson 'Company and his associates came to Ottawa and placed their views before the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister telephoned me at Winnipeg where I was on my 92582-170
way west, and I told him what it was. I heard no more regarding that speech except what appeared in the press; I heard no more of it until the 25th day of October last. The subject matter then came up.
I would not be at liberty to say what happened on that occasion except for this fact- and in this regard I should like to refer to an oath of office of a different character. There was given to the press what happened in cabinet council. The oath of office in that respect is rather complete. Without reading all, I will read a portion:
You will keep close and secret all such matters as shall be treated, debated, resolved on in privy council-
Etcetera, etcetera. I did not give out a single syllable, in any way, shape or form, of what happened there. The press had the story, and it was represented that I should either make apology or resign. I declined. There "is a question of misunderstanding. I am not going to debate that. The long and short of it was, I resigned from my seat in the cabinet, and I resigned as chairman of the commission because, as I stated in the correspondence that has been cited this afternoon, I felt it was desirable that the chairman of the commission should be one in harmony with the views of the government.
Now it has also been stated and charged by the right hon. gentleman-and it was suggested to-day-that I had made speeches regarding the work that was being carried on in the price spreads committee. That is perfectly true, and I did it deliberately. It was not done in a corner; I did it purposely. I knew very well that as a general rule matters of this kind referred to a committee of the House of Commons were bom to die, and I made up my mind that would not die. And it did not die. Again I say, sir, to you and to this house, that I make no apologies to anyone for the course I have pursued for the last fifteen months. I told the Prime Minister in January, 1934, a year ago last January, that knowing the conditions as I did, first among the agriculturists of this country, and the manner in which live stock particularly was under the dictation of large packing concerns, and having learned, secondly, the extent to which the sweatshop conditions of Canada had developed, I refused longer to remain silent on the subject. I declared to him, as I declared elsewhere on more than one occasion, that I proposed to raise my voice on every possible occasion so that the people of the country might know what the conditions were.

Price Spreads Commission

I have followed that policy deliberately and I propose still to follow it. It is said, sir, that I have violated-and this reference was made yesterday in an indirect way- judicial procedure. My answer to that is this: This was not a judicial inquiry. When this question first arose in January, 1934, following my speech in Toronto and following the protests of the T. Eaton Company regarding that speech, I asked for a judicial commission of inquiry, presided over by a judge. It was considered not advisable to appoint such a commission and the suggestion was made to me that a committee of the house should be set up, with myself as chairman, with full liberty to go into the matter as completely and freely as desired, and I accepted that responsibility. Had I done otherwise, I would have laid myself open to the charge that I was running away from a problem which I myself had cited. So I accepted -the responsibility, not as a .matter of choice, because I would have preferred a judicial inquiry.
But what happened? What happened was the appointment of a select special committee of the House of Commons of the ordinary type frequently appointed. That committee met and I was appointed its chairman. We carried on our work from February IS, I think it was, until the end of June. I believe hon. gentlemen will at least give that committee credit for this, that it was unremitting in its toil and devoted in its efforts to work out the problem submitted to it. It was appointed not as a judical inquiry with respect to any man, firm or business, but to investigate the cause of the low prices to the producer and the low wages to the worker, in addition to a number of other things that were recited. It was an investigation committee and I was chairman of that investigation committee. My duty was to investigate and not to sit as judge.
The right hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said as well that I had acted as judge, jury and prosecutor, and some of his followers have echoed that, shall I say, denunciation, the suggestion being that I had forgotten the duties of a judicial character and had been a prosecutor. Again I ask him or any other hon. member, in so far as I have acted as a prosecutor, to show me a single instance where I have been unjust to those who were brought before the tribunal? One thing I will say is: Whether they were rich or poor, whether they represented a great corporation or were employees of a great corporation, they got a fair deal before that committee but they got no more. It is true as I have said

that I have made a number, as a matter of fact, a great number of speeches, in Canada in which I reviewed those conditions. First I have tried to show to the public the facts of the case and the conditions which exist; second, I have endeavoured to suggest to the public possible remedial courses that might be adopted, and I have no hesitation in saying that to a measure at least the publicity which has been given to those speeches and to my activities in this respect has done something to mould public opinion along this line. To the extent that that has been done, I am content. My fate in this matter amounts to nothing. Whatever the right hon. gentleman's animus may be, I do not know what the cause of it is. I think I have sought to treat him, as I have tried to treat this house, with courtesy. I certainly differ on some subjects with some hon. gentlemen, some on this side and some on the other. There are viewpoints that are widely divergent. I respect their views, but I hold tenaciously to my own and I refuse at any time, as I have always done for the twenty-four years I have been in this house, to be a mere rubber stamp; if I have views, I will express them.
Since the committee was appointed in January, 1934, I have been subjected to all manner of criticism and opposition, and obstacles have been thrown in my way. I happen to know that thousands of dollars have been spent to try to find something that would discredit me. As I say, I have been in this house for twenty-four years; I have lived in Canada nearly all my life, about fifty years; I have lived in British Columbia for forty-one years, and I say to the right hon. gentleman now-and he has known me for a great many years-when he rises as a leader of a great party and impugns my honour, suggesting unethical and unfair practices, as he has done, I can look him or any other hon. member or anyone outside the house in the eye and say this:	While I am conscious of having made
many blunders and mistakes of which I am not proud, I can look the world in the face and assert: In so far as I have been able, I have conducted my course with at least a view to the honesty and decency of the game. It is true I have denounced certain practices. I have spoken, given expressions to views, and if I have an opportunity on a bill which I think is coming up here to-night in regard to amendments in connection with interest, I expect then to express views that will be distasteful to some of my friends through the country. I shall do this, because I feel it is in the interest of the country to do so, and I shall continue in that course. But because one remains silent as I have done for fifteen months

Price Spreads Commission
in regard to these matters, it does not follow that one is going to continue to do so and to allow others with impunity to attack one. No, I have no apologies to make to the right hon. gentleman, to this house or to anyone else for my conduct in connection with the price spreads committee last year or on the price spreads commission. I may have made mistakes, but I certainly have tried to do my duty as fearlessly and as frankly as I could do it.
