This question is raised as a matter of privilege and any member of the house concerned has a right to state his position. Yesterday I called attention to the fact that members of a royal commission are sworn in connection with the performance of their duties. Hon. members can read on the records of this house the form of oath which is administered. I wish to make one further reference in that connection, and that is that the order in council appointing the royal commission of which the hon. gentleman who last spoke (Mr. Stevens) was a member, provided that its members were to report their findings to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That was their express duty, and they were not to report their findings to representatives of the Toronto press.
With regard to other matters which were mentioned and in which I feel somewhat concerned, especially because the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is not here to justify the position which he took when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Stevens) resigned from the ministry, I desire to read from the correspondence in that connection something additional to what has been stated in the house. The Prime Minister in his letter dated October 26, 1934, addressed to the hon. gentleman who last spoke, which letter forms sessional paper No. 99 of the records of this house, said:
In consequence of my investigations and perusal of the pamphlet, I endeavoured to prevent its further circulation. I did so for two reasons:
1.	It is fundamentally unsound that the chairman of a select committee and of a royal commission, whether or not a member of the government, should publicly discuss the committee's proceedings before the evidence had been completed and' a report thereon made by the royal commission, especially in view of the rule that prevents members of the House of Commons from discussing in the house proceedings before its committees until final report has been made. Conclusions or judgments should not be pronounced until taking of evidence is completed and arguments heard thereon.
2.	Representations were made to me that statements contained in the pamphlet were at variance with the evidence given before the select committee, and were without any basis in fact. Circulation of such statements was
injurious not only to individuals and business institutions aggrieved thereby but also to yourself, and prejudicial to the effective work of the commission and' the cause you have so much at heart. I think you will agree that the circulation of a pamphlet containing untrue statements is contrary to every principle of British justice, and to pillory your fellow citizens in the court of public opinion on statements which are not supported by the evidence placed the commission as well as yourself and your colleagues in a most difficult position.
I do not propose to do more than direct your attention to the fact that it is now clear that the statements contained in your pamphlet with respect to several Canadian enterprises and individuals are untrue in whole or in part. About that, I think there can be not the slightest doubt. It is one thing for a private individual to express his opinion with respect to the solvency or insolvency of companies or persons or with respect to the value or lack of value of property owned by others; but when a minister of the crown, with all the authority and power of his position, makes statements which are at variance with the facts and which are not supported' by the evidence taken by the committee of which he is chairman, it is calculated to be most injurious to those concerned, and, as the minister is presumed to be speaking for the government, such action places upon the administration a grave and serious responsibility.
It is impossible to justify the publication and circulation of untrue statements by a minister of the crown which are calculated to have the effect of destroying the reputation or property of any citizen of the country. I do not propose to refer in detail to the inaccurate statements in question, to which your attention has already been directed.
And if it were not because of the privy council oath to which the hon. gentleman has referred one might state very clearly the matter to which the right hon. Prime Minister then referred; and he then continued:
Yesterday, in view of our previous discussions, I brought these matters to your attention as I deemed it desirable that you should indicate to me and to my colleague^ what course you proposed to pursue when the royal commission should meet next week. You were asked to state your views in the light of complaints that had been made by those who claim^ to have bben injured by misstatements contained in the pamphlet. You will recall that your colleagues were unanimously of the opinion that, in view of the inaccurate statements contained in the pamphlet, it was desirable, when the commission meets next week, that you should make a statement indicating the circumstances under which the pamphlet came into being, and expressing regret for any injury that such misstatements have caused to the reputation of any individual or business, and also indicating that the commission would afford complainants every opportunity to refute such misstatements.
I only wish to add that I can confirm from personal knowledge through being present on that occasion that what the Prime Minister there stated in that letter is entirely accurate.

The hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) 'has read a lengthy extract from a letter, part of a correspondence regarding my retirement from the cabinet, laying special emphasis on certain paragraphs in that letter, which by the way has been on the table of the house for some months. I now claim the privilege of reading my reply to that letter. I did not invite this but I will not run away from it.
This is a letter dated October 30, 1934, and directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada:
Dear Prime Minister:-
Your letter dated October 26, accepting my resignation, was delivered to me at my home by special messenger at 4.30 Saturday afternoon, the 27th instant.
In your letter you seek to establish that in my work -as chairman of the "price spreads and mass buying committee" I had enjoyed the full support of my colleagues of the government. This, sir, you know is not true.
From the moment of the organization of the committee, following my speech in Toronto on January 15 last, almost daily throughout the long period of the last session I was subjected to -irritating criticisms. One day it would be regarding my manner as chairman, the next the treatment of witnesses, particularly that of Stanley McLean of Canada Packers and of the heads of the Imperial Tobacco. Then the question of cost was constantly thrown in my face, and through it all from one of your senior members ran the constant refrain in a minor key "What can you do about it anyway?"
The fact that I refused to be influenced by these mischievous interferences is now advanced by you as evidence that I had an "absolutely free hand." In the interests of simple truth I must protest your claim in that respect, for, on the contrary, there has been constant criticism emanating almost exclusively from a small minority of the cabinet who, together with yourself, now seize on the "pamphlet" as a culminating excuse for an unwarranted attack on me as chairman of the commission and as a minister of the crown.
You express regret that I did not take the course suggested by you and your colleagues. It is always proper to make amends for any injustice done and none would be more ready to do this than I would be. For me, however, to have acted on your suggestion would have effectively destroyed my usefulness in the task I have set myself, and I would have been false to what I believed to be true and in the public interest. It would have been tantamount to a complete capitulation to those interests whose business practices are in my opinion responsible for untold suffering amongst the agricultural and industrial population of this country.
Making the apology you suggested would have been an easy way for me to have retained my seat in the cabinet but I prize my liberty of action and my sense of duty to the public of

Canada more than the mere retention of office.
It was not this only that caused me to tender my resignation; but rather the intolerable conditions which had developed in connection with my work as chairman of the commission and a minister of the crown.
I deeply resent-
As I do now.
[DOT]-your thinly veiled insinuation that I have been deliberately untruthful. In this respect you base your judgment on representations from one whom you fail to name in your communication, nor have you offered a scintilla of evidence to support your innuendo. In conversation, but n-ot in your letter, you told me that you rest your case on representations made to you in the early part of August last by C. L. Burton, head of the Simpson Company^ Limited. You further stated that he had submitted to you documentary support for his allegations. Would it not have been an act of courtesy to have submitted these documents to me for answer?
And I interject that up to the present moment I have not been accorded the courtesy of the alleged documentary evidence.
Furthermore, you did not speak to me about this matter from August 4 until Thursday afternoon last-
That was October 25.
-which again, I suggest, is a singular course of action to adopt towards a colleague.
My public utterances have been made for the purpose of informing the people of Canada of grave social and economic wrongs which, as a result of my study of their causes, I believe are due largely to certain practices indulged in by large merchandising concerns.
I have under my hand indubitable support for what I have said but I choose to reserve extended and detailed discussions for the public platform and the floor of parliament.
As to the propriety of my actions as chairman of the price spreads committee last session, I prefer to leave this to the judgment of the public for whose opinion I still entertain great respect. But, sir, why all the reticence about discussing these subjects? As a matter of fact full account of the evidence

I ask the house to note this.
-had already been exhaustively reported and reviewed in the public press.
That is a matter which is ignored to-day. Full reports of the proceedings of the committee were published on the front pages of all the papers of Canada, and all I did was deal with matters that already had been in the public press to a very wide extent.
The front page of every large daily -in Canada had from week to week carried' the story, and all of this, months before the "pamphlet" was ever heard of.
In your letter to me you were good enough to express some words of appreciation-
Which, by the way, were carefully excluded by the hon. gentleman who just spoke.

Price Spreads Commission
-of my work as a minister. These words I acknowledge with thanks. But, sir, when you refer in your closing words to "British justice and fair play" I cannot hut bring to my mind the countless thousands of citizens of Canada who are patiently suffering while others whom you champion in such eloquent terms have been reaping rewards far beyond that which any citizen might reasonably expect to win. It is for those inarticulate sufferers that I have been striving with the hope that remedial measures might be found.
There was a further letter which in justice to the Prime Minister I will also read. I regret that this correspondence between the Prime Minister and myself should be introduced while he was absent, but it was not done by me; let that be noted. The Prime Minister's reply was dated October 31:
I received your letter of yesterday in due course.
As you resigned _ as Minister of Trade and Commerce and chairman of the royal commission rather than resume, as proposed, the amicable discussion with your then colleagues, which, by consent, -was adjourned on Thursday last-
I will deal with that in a moment.
-when all relevant papers to which you refer were available to you, no useful purpose will be served by anticipating parliamentary discussion and containing the correspondence with respect to events of which I think it proper to state that your indicated memory is at variance with the recollection of my colleagues and myself.
I wish to refer to these words:
*-the amicable discussion with your then colleagues-
It has been stated, and I welcome this opportunity of making a statement in this regard, that my colleagues desired me to return and discuss the matter further, or to put it more accurately, perhaps, that cabinet council adjourned with the expectation of meeting again the next day and continuing the discussion. That is perfectly true, but on the morning of the 26th, before noon-and the cabinet council was to reassemble in the afternoon-to my annoyance I found that there appeared in the press a fairly complete resume of wlhat had happened in council, in regard to which a very solemn oath had been taken. The gist of this publication was that I had been asked to make some amends, and to whom? To Mr. C. L. Burton, of the Robert Simpson Company, and one other firm that was never mentioned in- the price spreads committee but which I mentioned here in the House of Commons during the debate on the budget last year. I will leave them out. I was asked to make amends to C. L. Burton, of the Robert Simpson Company, who had complained to the Prime
Minister regarding the utterances in the pamphlet, to which I shall make further reference in a moment. And the newspaper account of the meeting of the cabinet was to the effect that if I did not make these amends I would be asked to resign. Sir,
I would not take that position for anybody, and I resigned and refused to go back to cabinet under those conditions. I resigned for that purpose and for that reason, that the secret and private discussions of cabinet had been spread upon the pages of the press. Had I gone back and had an amicable arrangement been made between my colleagues and myself it would have been on record that I had gone back because I had been publicly spanlked in the press, and I had no intention of placing myself in that humiliating position. That was why I did not go back to cabinet council.
Now I should like to say a word with reference to the Robert Simpson Company and Mr. Burton. The Prime Minister, in the correspondence read by the Secretary of State with such unction, said there were certain misstatements in the pamphlet. I have the pamphlet here. One of the alleged misstatements was this, that the Robert Simpson Company, who at the time they did that splendid piece of financing-from the standpoint of Sir Joseph Flavelle and all the crowd-which permitted the original group to take $10,000,000 out of the company and substitute for it a lot of mortgage bonds, all of which is in this report which will be tabled to-day, bearing out to the letter what I am saying and what I said in this pamphlet; in that financial set-up they issued $10,000,000 of bonds, and then they issued A and B stock-

Mr. Speaker, I was in the middle of a sentence referring to the refinancing of the Robert Simpson Company, to which

reference was made in this pamphlet which is the basis of all the accusations made in that letter regarding truthfulness or otherwise. I had said that in that refinancing structure they issued $10,000,000 of bonds, $10,000,000 of preference stocks, and two other classes of stock, one A common and one B common, one at $50 a share and the other I think at $100 a share. In any .case there was a class A and a class B common, about $2,000,000 of that, and speaking from memory $1,800,000 was sold to the employees, and was sold to the employees under conditions which were anything but fair to them or a credit to the company. Many of those employees are still paying for that stock at $50 a share although the stock to-day is virtually worthless, being quoted on occasion at $5 for the class B and $10 for .the class A, but I am told by brokers upon inquiry, and I have made inquiries, that it was without real value because there is no sale for it. But in my pamphlet I said that it was class B stock that the employees got. The truth is that it was class A stock, and so I am branded as being untruthful for the difference between A and B. I will admit it.
Another statement that I was charged with being untruthful in is this. In my speech before hon. members of the study club, referring to this matter I said that this stock was not worth a snap of your finger; that is the way I described it. I was told afterwards that that was a grossly unfair statement because the stock was worth $5 in the one case and $10 in the other, although it had been sold to these poor employees at $50 a share. I said it was not worth a snap of your finger, and again I was branded with being untruthful for that.
I went through this pamphlet, and I have here a list of the statements I made, but I shall not go into that now. I went back over the auditors' report and I took every one of these statements, and with the exception of these two to which I have referred, the transposing of A for B and the failure to interpret in printed form a snap of the finger, for that I was branded.
The other instance was where I referred to the Steelwares Company. That had nothing to do with the commission, nothing whatever to do with it, never was before it. I said in my place in the house beside the Prime Minister last session, speaking in the budget debate, that there had been 120 mergers in this country between 1920 and 1930. I made an analysis of them and I cited about a dozen, and among the companies I cited was the Steelwares Company. It was referred to again

Price Spreads Commission
in that speech which I made and which later became this pamphlet, and on that account again I was branded as being untruthful. I take back nothing that I said there. This thing has been before the public for six months, and I take nothing back. What I was arguing for is this, and I shall argue it further; I was arguing against the growing tendency in Canada of the concentration of the control of credit and the control of industry in the hands of a few, which makes it impossible for the agriculturist or for the individualist successfully to compete.
Yesterday afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I was absent from my seat in the house when this question was raised. I was in my office discussing with one of the outstanding private manufacturers of Canada-what? This man has built up an excellent business, has no mortgage on his plants, no bond issues. He has built up an excellent business; he is one of the ablest exporters and manufacturers in Canada, and he stands to-day confronted with a condition which indicates the ruination of his business. Why? Because a great American concern with a branch in this country with twenty or thirty million dollars of assets has gone into the banking business and is furnishing two and three years' credit to customers in Canada and driving this man, who is unable to grant such credit, out of business. And, sir, when he goes to the Canadian banks to borrow money he is asked seven and six per cent for it, while the customers of the American concern with a branch in Canada are getting it for five per cent. How can the Canadian survive? I was sitting in my office discussing that matter when this question came up yesterday or I should have been here. I merely state that, Mr. Speaker, in support of what I say has been behind this thing and what is behind it now, and if this house will address itself to the study of the problem of the concentration of power and wealth in this country, instead of to the Lilliputian performance of yesterday the house would be better off.

IMr. Stevens,]
I consider myself fortunate in being called upon in his stead on this occasion. Representing Canada as I did for some years in the United Kingdom, I had the great privilege of coming into frequent personal contact with His Majesty, and I share with all those who have had a similar privilege, feelings of great admiration and profound respect as well as of loyal devotion. As the house may know, I was High Commissioner and Minister of Overseas Military Forces of Canada during a very trying period of His Majesty's rule; a period when the fortunes of his throne and of his empire were put to the stern test of armed conflict.
In the storm and stress of those difficult times, His Majesty gave his people the inspiration of great leadership, steady optimism and self-sacrificing devotion. Without ostentation, he kept in the closest possible touch with all the activities of his people. He visited the training camps, the armies in France and Belgium, the fleet at S'capa Flow, munitions plants throughout the country, and hospitals and convalescent homes. As I was privileged to be present on many of these occasions I can assure the house from personal knowledge that his simple human sympathy and his calm unremitting devotion to duty cheered and steadied the country. In all these things the king was always assisted and supported by Her Gracious Majesty the Queen and so in those dark days of war, as well as in the even more difficult tests of peace that followed, Their Majesties won for themselves, once and for all, an imperishable place in the hearts and minds of the people of the whole British commonwealth.
There is no doubt but that it was the character and conduct of His Majesty throughout these testing times that led to the strengthening of the monarchy with us at the very time that it was breaking down elsewhere. Since the war, thrones throughout Europe have toppled and the established order has been uprooted. The throne of His Majesty has remained secure and has in fact become more firmly based. The crown for us is the symbol not of despotism but of constitutional liberty and ordered progress; not of autocratic empire but of the voluntary union of free states.
'Constitutional relations within the empire have changed much since the accession of His Majesty. The relation of the dominions and the United Kingdom is no longer that of colony to mother country, but of self-governing nations freely associated with each other. This development, however, far from weakening the position of the crown has only served to

Address to His Majesty
strengthen, it. The throne now more definitely than ever before binds us to one another and to our past. From whatever part of the empire we may come, we all claim kinship through our common allegiance to Hi3 Majesty the King,
His Majesty's reign has been eventful for more developments than the war and the constitutional evolution of the 'British commonwealth of nations. I shall not attempt to pass in review the events of these crowded twenty-five years, but I think I am safe in saying that there has never been a more dynamic, a more significant, a more difficult quarter century since recorded history began. In dealing with the baffling problems caused by these rapid social and political changes, His Majesty's ministers had at all times the benefit of His Majesty's ripe judgment, long experience and wise advice.
Many years ago a wise commentator on the British constitution, Walter Bagehot, stated " a sovereign has, under a constitutional monarchy such as ours, three rights- the right to be consulted, the right to encourage, the right to warn. And a king of great sense and sagacity would want no others-perhaps such powers as these are what a wise man would most seek to exercise and least fear to possess."
It is in the exercise of these powers that our king has played and continues to play his part in guiding the destinies of this great array of peoples who make up the British empire.
I do not feel that I need say any more. Inadequate as my words have been, they are the sincere expression of what I know animates every member of this house and every citizen of this country; loyal and affectionate devotion to His Majesty the King and Her Majesty the Queen.
I therefore move, seconded by Mr. Mackenzie King:
That an humble address be voted to His Majesty the King in the following words:- To the King's Most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, Your Majesty's loyal and dutiful subjects,
the House of Commons of Canada in parliament assembled, beg to offer our sincere congratulations on the happy completion of the twenty-fifth year of your illustrious reign.
The eventful years which have passed since Your Majesty's accession to the throne have witnessed great and significant changes in economic, social and political conditions that have constantly demanded the exercise of the highest qualities of courage and of leadership. During these years important and definite developments in the constitutional relations between the several parts of Your Majesty's dominions have more firmly established that unity of which their common allegiance to the
crown is the symbol and inspiration. We rejoice that each year has been marked by an increasing appreciation of Your Majesty's inspiring example of conscientious devotion to duty and of unselfish labour for the welfare of your people. Your Majesty will celebrate the twenty-fifth anniversary of your accession enjoying the unreserved respect and the loyal affection of the people in all parts of your dominions, which is a striking demonstration of the righteousness and wisdom which Your Majesty has exhibited both in war and in peace through years of unexampled difficulty.
We ask that our loyal and respectful congratulations may be accepted by Her Gracious Majesty the Queen whose untiring interest in every movement for the relief of distress and suffering and' for the welfare of humanity has given her a secure place in the affections of the people of Canada. We rejoice that the queen will share the demonstration of loyalty and devotion which will be shown to Your Majesty on this memorable anniversary.
From time to time during Your Majesty's reign the people of Canada have enjoyed the honour of welcoming to this dominion His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales and other members of the Royal family, whose visits have not only deepened the loyal devotion of the [DOT]people of Canada to Your Majesty but have enhanced their appreciation of the interest which is always taken by the members of the Royal family in all that pertains to the progress and welfare of this dominion.
We trust that we may continue for many years to enjoy the benefit of your gracious and peaceful rule. Our earnest prayer is that He who is the Ruler of all nations and the King of Kings may uphold, direct and preserve Your Majesty in health, in happiness, and in the affectionate loyalty of your people.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
In rising to
second the motion which has just been made by the right hon. the acting leader of the house (Sir George Perley), may I say immediately that I share with him very sincerely the regret which he has expressed that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is himself prevented from being in the house and having the honour of moving the address which has just been read. I hope, as I know all hon. members of this house also hope, that there may be some compensation to the Prime Minister in the fact that in all probability he will have an opportunity of personally presenting to His Majesty the address which is being voted by both houses of this parliament on the occasion of the celebration of the silver jubilee of His Majesty's accession to the throne. May I say further, seeing that it is impossible for the Prime Minister, to be here to have the honour of moving the address, that I am very pleased, as I am sure all hon. members of this house are, that that honour has fallen to one who has played such a long and honourable part in the public life of our country as my right hon. friend the acting
Address to His Majesty

leader of the house has; and one, moreover, who has been privileged, in the course of his distinguished and self-effacing career, to have the Close official and personal relations with His Majesty the King which my right hon. friend has enjoyed.
It affords me, Mr. Speaker, much pleasure to have the honour of seconding the address which has just been moved by the right hon. the acting leader of the government to His Majesty King George V, congratulating His Majesty upon the completion of the twenty-fifth year of his reign. The sentiments expressed in the address are so completely in accord with those cherished towards His Majesty by the citizens of Canada generally, that it would only detract from the felicity of their expression were I to attempt to supplement, at any length, what appears in the address, and what has been so appropriately said by the acting leader of the government in proposing the motion.
May I say that I nevertheless welcome the courtesy extended by the government, in inviting me to second the address, in that it affords one of those occasions, too rare in our parliamentary life, where it is possible to make apparent that, however much members of the official opposition in this House of Commons may differ from hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to the policies which are best suited to the government of our country, as representatives of the people of Canada, we are, at all times, one with them in our allegiance to the crown, and are particularly so to-day, in the congratulations being extended from the parliament of Canada to His Majesty.
In the world's history there has been nothing comparable to the past twenty-five years. In this momentous epoch, the nations of the British commonwealth have indeed been fortunate in having so wise and good a king. I believe it is impossible to over-estimate how much, within this period, British peoples the world over, and indeed the world itself, owe to the personality, and to the personal example of King George, to His Majesty's steadfastness, his understanding, his fidelity and his sagacity.
As the address says, "in war and in peace, through years of unexampled difficulty," King George has been an exemplary sovereign. He has worked with his people, as well as for them. Their fortunes have been his, and his theirs.
In the great war, His Majesty, not less because of his own personal example, than in virtue of his high office, stood as the symbol of the common effort of all parts

of his dominions. He was the rallying centre of all the forces that, in His Majesty's name, and in the name of British liberty, fought for a larger freedom. As other thrones have crashed and crumbled, his throne has become more firmly established.
In the difficult post-war period of reconstruction, as governments have come and gone, and many constitutional changes have been effected, His Majesty, in virtue of his understanding and wisdom, has remained the embodiment of an unswerving constitutional authority in Great Britain and beyond the seas.
Having regard to the times, and to the issues King George and his ministers have been called upon to face, I 'believe it can honestly be said that there has never been a better king.
It is most fitting that, in the address to His Majesty on this occasion, congratulations should be conveyed, as well, to Her Majesty the Queen, and that, as has been done, reference should be made to the place held by Her Majesty in the affections of the people. We are fully conscious of what, in sickness and in health, and in all that pertains to his high office, the life partnership of Her Majesty the Queen has meant to the king.
May I, in conclusion, say within these halls of parliament, what, recently, I was privileged to say beyond its walls:
"We welcome the opportunity, which this anniversary affords, to pay our tribute alike to the king and queen, to their sincere love for the people, their self-sacrificing lives, their definite standards of right and wrong, their simplicity of heart, and their steadfast faith. At this time, we are deeply conscious of what all these have meant to us, to our country, to the British commonwealth of nations, and to the world."

It
is indeed with pleasure that I rise to support the motion that an address be presented to His Majesty congratulating him upon the twenty-fifth anniversary of his accession to the throne. This motion has been so well spoken to by the acting leader of the house (Sir George Per-ley) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) that it is not necessary for me to do more than say that on this historic occasion I am sure we as members of the house can forget our differences of opinion in order that we may speak with a united voice. I am certain it is the wish of all that His Majesty will retain his health and strength so that he may long remain in the prominent position which he now occupies.

Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to create employment by public works and undertakings throughout Canada, and to authorize the government to guarantee equipment securities of the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Company in the amount of fifteen million dollars.
He said:	His Excellency the Governor
General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Perhaps this
is the appropriate time to draw to the attention of the house what seems to me to be a curious procedure with respect to this particular motion. It is in the name of the Prime Minister, but it relates to a measure that is to create employment by public works and undertakings throughout Canada, and also to authorize the government to guarantee equipment securities of the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Company in the amount of 815,000,000. My first observation is that the motion relates to two separate and distinct measures, and this house should have two different bills presented to it, one which will deal with the question of the creation of employment by public works and undertakings and the other which relates to the guarantees to the railways of their equipment securities.
I further think the correct procedure would be that any measure relating to the construction of public works should be brought in by the Minister of Public Works, and that
a measure relating to the guarantee of equipment securities of railways should be introduced by the Minister of Railways. I would much rather say what I am about to say with the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) present, but it is necessary to speak at once in order to bring out what I think is important in the matter of the procedure that we have been adopting of late. I cannot understand how it is, with the Prime Minister absent, and1 necessarily so, from the house since February 22, and, as we have been told by the acting leader of the government (Sir George Perley), quite unable to take and, I am sure, not taking any part in the business of the government, so many measures should continue to be introduced in the house in the name of the Prime Minister.
The theory of responsible government is that it is a ministry that is responsible, the ministers are responsible. The Prime Minister is simply the first among equals. I do think that if the theory of responsible gov-mmeat is to foe adhered to, measures that immediately affect particular departments of government should appear in the names of the ministers who are -responsible for those departments and who are the only ones present in parliament to discuss those measures. I would draw the attention of my right hon. friend to the fa-ct that since February 22 we have had submitted to this house or introduced a resolution with respect to the Canadian grain board which is in the name of the Prime Minister. I think that measure would more properly appear in the name of either the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Agriculture. Then there was a resolution with regard to the economic council of Canada; as it refers more particularly to the Prime Minister's department possibly it -might foe supposed to be introduced by the Prime Minister, but in the circumstances I think it might quite properly have been in the name of the Secretary of State. Then we have had several labour measures. We have one on the order -paper still, placed there on March 6, in respect to the creation of minimum wage fixing machinery. This is in the name of the Prime Minister, I think it should have been in the name of the Minister of Labour. We have had a weekly day of rest bill, we have had an eight hour day bill and other measures relating distinctly to labour, which in the circumstances would more properly have been in the name of the minister of the department concerned. Then on March 8 there was introduced a bill respecting the additional protocol -of 1935 to the Canada-
Public Works Program

France trade agreement. That surely was a matter for the Minister -of Trade and Commerce, or, seeing that the Secretary of State had to do with the negotiation of part of it, it might have been in his name, but I think should have appeared in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Now we have this particular measure which is certainly public works and railways; why it should be in the name of the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Public Works should take charge of it, I cannot understand.
I sometimes fear -that we are completely changing the character of our political institutions, and amongst other things that little by little in this parliament we are following what I think is a mistaken method becoming common in Europe, of having the leader of a political party assume responsibility for all measures, and other ministers reduced to mere ciphers, in the part which they are to take in the proceedings of parliament and in discussion of public questions. I bring the matter up now because I think it is time that attention should be called to what is certainly an irregular procedure. I know the acting Prime Minister is here, and it is quite right that any measure that pertains to the Prime Minister's office should be introduced by him and dealt with by him, but when it comes to a position such as we have this afternoon, where a measure is in the name of the Prime Minister and the acting Prime Minister leaves it to other .colleagues to deal with, I submit it is obvious that there is something not wholly in aocord with the theory of collective responsibility on the part of the ministry and the direct responsibility of certain ministers.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. C. MATTHEWS (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Yesterday on the orders of the day the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) inquired as to the practice of the Department of National Revenue in recording the return to Canada of Canadian butter exported to Great Britain. For the information of the hon. member I may say that butter exported from Canada to Great Britain and returned to Canada falls within two categories:
1.	Canadian butter which has been shipped to England and returned to the exporter in Canada within five years without having

Mounted Police
changed ownership or having advanced in value, on arriving in Canada and being duly identified, a free import entry is made, under the provisions of tariff item 709; but no segregation of the different kinds of goods entered under this item is made for statistical purposes.
2.	Canadian butter exported to Great Britain which has entered into ordinary commerce and has thereby lost its identity or has changed ownership or increased in value. On return to Canada this butter, subject to payment of duty would be recorded as an importation from the United Kingdom, without identification as to country of origin.
When Canadian goods are returned, whether entered free or subject to duty, the original export entry stands without cancellation. This applies to all goods, including butter. It will accordingly be apparent that so far as the Department of National Revenue is concerned it is not possible to furnish statistics with respect to the quantity of Canadian butter which may have been returned to Canada during any particular year. The practice I have indicated has been in vogue under tariff item 709 since the year 1906.

I
merely wish to state that I am pleased that the minister has submitted this statement. It bears out what I thought the customs law was, that no goods of any kind enter Canada, either as Canadian goods returned or otherwise, without an import entry. That is the point I wished to make.
Quite right.

subtopic: USE OF DOGS TO LOCATE LOST PERSONS BUT NOT TO TRACK CRIMINALS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: USE OF DOGS TO LOCATE LOST PERSONS BUT NOT TO TRACK CRIMINALS
speechtext:
On March 29 I asked a question with regard to the reported use by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police of bloodhounds to locate persons lost in Nova Scotia forests and to track criminals. I asked whether the full cabinet had given their consent to this method of tracking down criminals, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) replied that the answer was in the negative. I then asked further as to whether this proceeding had been sanctioned by the government, and the Minister of Justice replied it had not. I notice in the Montreal Herald of April 11 a dispatch from Winnipeg, as follows:
"Bloodhounds" are now being used by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, General J. H. MacBrien, chief commissioner, said here to-day, but only for tracking purposes. Recently the
matter was brought up in the House of Commons. The dogs, Genera.l MacBrien said, are not used in the manner depicted in dime novel "thrillers" and he deprecated any idea that fugitives might be torn limb from limb by ferocious canines.
My question is this: If the government does not sanction this proceeding, does Major General MacBrien consider himself above the laiw, -or will the government take suitable action to enforce its position upon Major General MacBrien?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: USE OF DOGS TO LOCATE LOST PERSONS BUT NOT TO TRACK CRIMINALS
speechtext: When the question was asked previously I stated that the government had not authorized the use of bloodhounds in connection with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I can repeat that statement; there are no bloodhounds used by the mounted police. I think a similar statement appeared in another newspaper, in which General MacBrien says these are not bloodhounds. I made inquiries with respect to the matter immediately after it was brought up in the house previously. There are some small dogs- they are down at Rockcliffe and can be seen by anyone-called pinschers, German dogs, and I believe there is a German sheep dog as well. Experience has shown that these are the most valuable dogs for tracing missing persons; it is said they have the most acute sense of smell of any dogs. They are little fellows; they are used chiefly for finding lost children or people who have strayed in the woods. They are not used at all in this country for tracking criminals; they are not set loose but are used exclusively on the leash. The policeman, or whoever is sent to find the lost person, takes the dog and follows it after it has located the scent. We have a few of these dogs down at Rockcliffe and we propose to endeavour to use them in finding lost or strayed persons. A number of them have been successfully used in the west, and we believe it will be of some value to have some of these dogs for the use of the force. I repeat that they are not bloodhounds.

subtopic: BILL BASED ON DRAFT CONVENTION OF INTERNATIONAL LABOUR ORGANIZATION AND TREATY OF VERSAILLES

speechtext:
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 40, to provide for minimum wages pursuant to the convention concerning minimum wages adopted by the international labour organization in accordance with the provisions of part XIII of the treaty of Versailles and of the corresponding parts of the other treaties of peace.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BILL BASED ON DRAFT CONVENTION OF INTERNATIONAL LABOUR ORGANIZATION AND TREATY OF VERSAILLES
speechtext: The bill is drawn pursuant to the draft convention of the general conference of the international labour organization of the League of Nations, which convention has been adopted by this house during the present session. The bill professes to follow as closely as possible, having regard to the situation, the draft convention which was submitted, and the plan under the bill is, briefly, to appoint a committee to consist of a minister, being the Minister of Labour, a representative of the employer and a representative of the employees in each particular trade, to fix a minimum wage to be paid in respect of that trade throughout the dominion. The treaty itself provides that the bill shall not became operative until after the lapse of one year after its deposit at Geneva, and a special clause is inserted to provide that in the interval before it becomes law, in any exceptional case, the governor in council may provide a minimum wage after having made inquiry as set out in the terms of the bill. Otherwise I think the bill follows pretty closely the language of the treaty which was approved by the house at the present session.

subtopic: BILL BASED ON DRAFT CONVENTION OF INTERNATIONAL LABOUR ORGANIZATION AND TREATY OF VERSAILLES
speechtext:
I have listened to the
minister's explanation with regard to this bill. I wish to assure hon. members that I am among the first members of the house who have studied the question of minimum wages. I did so away back in 1928 with the assistance of Hon. Peter Heenan, Minister of Labour at that time, and also the very valuable help of my revered leader, because I was just starting to make a study of statistics and very often I had to go to the right hon. gentleman for advice. I wish to express my thanks to him in that- connection.
This bill is supposed to be based upon a draft convention which appeared on the orders

Minimum Wage
of the day of March 11 of this year. It is a draft convention and just a moment ago I heard the Minister of Justice repeat the statement that it was. I have asked for the book in which that draft convention could be found and my first question was to the acting Prime Minister. My question was asked on March 11 last, as reported on page 1573 of Hansard, and the fact that the right hon. gentleman had time enough to think before answering me is apparent in that the answer was given on the following day as reported on page 1616. He read an answer in which it was stated:
The texts of draft conventions and recommendations adopted by international labour conferences are not printed in the official journal of the League of Nations but are to be found in the official bulletin of the international labour office where, on page 121 of the issue of the 31st July, 1928, he will find the text of _ the convention concerning the creation of minimum wage fixing machinery.
This was not in the journals of the League of Nations. I have the official bulletin referred to by the right hon. gentleman, and at page 121, the page he mentioned, there are only three lines and four words, as follows:
Minimum wage fixing machinery.
And they refer to another booklet entitled:
Second discussion; international labour convention; eleventh session, Geneva, May 1928; report on minimum wage fixing machinery; first item on the agenda; international labour office, Geneva, 1928.
This booklet, which has 149 pages, I have procured from the library.
On March 19, a week after I had received the answer from the acting Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice referred me to another book which he was kind enough to lend me, but it was not the book mentioned by the acting Prime Minister, nor the one that I hold in my hand. He mentioned another book, and he brought into the matter a dark horse, a third book which contained draft conventions; in fact it was called, Draft Conventions and Recommendations Adopted by the International Labour Conference at its sessions from 1919 to 1932.
But the most important point that I wish to stress is this: that the acting Prime Minister, the present leader of the government, has referred me to the page of that booklet, the official bulletin of the international labour office of July 31, 1928, which refers to the book already described that I now hold in my hand, this one containing 149 pages. This means that this book is the basis of the legislation which is now before us. The importance of this is the way in which this country has
answered the questions which have been put by the international labour conference. These are several questions which appear on page 2:
Principle of the creation of machinery and scope of its application.
1.	Do you consider that the conference should adopt proposals dealing with methods of minimum wage fixing in home working and other trades or in parts of such trades in which:
(a)	No arrangements exist for the effective regulation of wages by collective agreement or otherwise, and
(b)	Wages are exceptionally low?
2.	Do you consider that a definition of (a) home working trades, and (b) other trades, should be included in any proposals which may be adopted by the conference? What definitions do you propose?
3.	Do you consider that it is for the government of each country to decide, having regard to the conditions of the country, which are the home working and other trades covered by question one?
4.	What criteria (if any) would you propose to adopt for determining in which trades there are:
(a)	No arrangements for the effective regulation of wages;
(b)	Exceptionally low wages?
There are first answers from Austria and Belgium, then the answer from Canada. Was it given by the Canadian government? No, It was given first by British Columbia; second, by Manitoba; third, by Ontario and, fourth, by Quebec. This means that the government of that day, respecting the ruling of the Supreme Court of Canada, had decided not themselves to answer the question on behalf of the federal government, but to submit the questions to the provinces, and then the answers were sent back to the federal government and later forwarded to Geneva. This shows that the former Liberal government respected the confederation pact and acted under its provisions in regard to this important matter.
This is not the only question which was asked. There are several others, and I shall read a few of them to show that the former Liberal government were sincere in saying that when those matters were to be settled, they had to be settled in conformity with the law of the land. Another question is as follows:
Question 5:
Basis for fixing minimum wages.
Do you consider that some provision should be made for a basis for fixing minimum wages? If so, what basis do you suggest?
This is answered by Austria, Belgium, Canada. The answer for Canada is given by British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, as reported on pages 38 and 39 of this book.
2688
Minimum Wage

Other questions of similar importance come afterward:
Determination of the minimum wage fixing methods.
6.	Do you consider that the conference should:
(a)	Lay down the method or methods upon which the minimum wages should he fixed? If so, what method or methods do you propose? Or
(b)	Confine itself to laying down general principles? If so, what principles do you suggest?
7.	If not, do you consider that it is for the government of each country to decide, having regard to the administrative practice of the country, the method or methods to be introduced in fixing minimum wages in the home working or other trades covered by question one?
This is answered by Austria, Belgium and Canada. For Canada the answer is not given by the federal government. It is given for Canada by the provinces of British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec. And there are other questions of some importance with regard to the same matter; question 8 on page 52:
Do you consider that any such method should make provision for full preliminary consultation with representatives of the trade concerned, including representatives of organizations of employers and workers (if any), and with any other persons specially qualified by their trade or functions to be usefully consulted?
Answered for Canada by British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec.
9.	Do you consider that employers and workers should be represented on the wage fixing body? If so, do you consider that they should be represented' in equal numbers?
10.	Do you consider that any minimum wage fixing body should contain an independent person or persons?
11.	What methods do you consider should be adopted in selecting and appointing:
(a)	the representatives of employers and workers;
(b)	the independent person or persons?
Answered for Canada by the four provinces already named.
12.	What systems of inspection, general supervision and enforcement do you propose for insuring the payment of wages in the trades concerned at not less than the rates fixed?
The same answer, by the four provinces already mentioned.
13.	Do you consider that the government should communicate to the international labour office, either in the annual report furnished in accordance with article 408 of the treaty or otherwise in the case of a recommendation, the list of trades in which the system of fixing minimum wages has been applied, together with the approximate number of workers covered, and a general statement on the minimum rates of wages and other conditions established in the trades concerned?

The same answer for Canada by the four provinces already mentioned.
14.	Do you consider that the conference should proceed by way of a draft convention or a recommendation or both? If the latter, in what respects should either form of decision be adopted?
The same answer for Canada by the four provinces already mentioned.
Then there is a general survey of the question in the light of the replies of the governments. But the government in this instance was not the federal government, it was each provincial government. Some of them did not answer, but the answers which were given were in accordance with the ruling of the supreme court of this country. It is all very well to say, "We will change the social order." The social order cannot be changed so easily as that; it cannot be changed by the will of one man, however powerful he may be. It is a matter of great importance that things be done rightly; no one can escape the obligation to follow the right path. It would have been easy for the previous government to pass legislation such as this, but it was repugnant to their sense of duty to the people of this country. I believe in minimum wages; I have advocated them, and it was after the statistics which I compiled were submitted to this house and studied by the Minister of Labour of the time, who was very earnest in that regard, that an act was passed by this parliament to establish minimum wages for the men employed directly by the federal government. The federal government could not go further than that on account of the ruling of the court.
Sir, I am strongly in favour of minimum wages being applied throughout the country from one ocean to the other, and the sooner it becomes a reality the better. But if it comes it must come to serve a useful purpose, not to deceive the people. As this legislation is drafted it rests upon nothing. The very fact that it is based on the report which I have just read shows that this parliament has no jurisdiction at all in the matter. The very basis of it is the reference which has been given by the acting Prime Minister. It is most interesting to go to the rock bottom of things; there we find the truth, but at times it takes a lot of digging and excavation to discover it. When the truth is discovered no one can do otherwise than fight for it. The truth is that this legislation is- built on sand, on the sand of d(?beit. I know very well what will happen in the next election; hon. members to your right, sir, will tell the working men of this country, who are exploited: "Here we are to save you with new legislation which will increase your wages." But as soon as a

Minimum Wage
manufacturer attacks this legislation before the courts, the judiciary will do the same work as I have done; he will go to the bottom of it-if he does not he will not fulfil his duty- and he will see that this parliament has no jurisdiction whatever in this matter. Sir, that is a very serious statement to make; I make it only after having gone to the source of this legislation as presented by the acting Prime Minister. There may be some harebrained clerks in the civil service who pretend to do more than they are capable of, who bring to this government half-baked legislation, telling them that they have gone through all the previous legislation, but that serves no useful purpose. It is only deceit, and those men who have drafted this legislation deserve to be discharged at once, because it is bad, it is not even sensible, it rests on nothing and is just misleading to the working men of this country.
The government complain that there have been profiteers who have taken advantage of the working men in order to pay small wages. I admit that. But who protected these manufacturers by high tariffs since 1930? The government have done the same as the packing business; they have been fattening hogs since 1930, and now that the hogs are fat they try to kill them. We heard the Prime Minister declare at the special session of 1930 that as a result of raising the tariff there would be no unemployment in this country. The reason the tariff was raised was to decrease unemployment, we were told. What was the result? To-day the figures of unemployment are astounding. We have not yet got the whole truth in that matter, but we shall get it, and we shall see that it is most important to follow the right path of law and jurisprudence in order to do something for the working men of this country who need help. But the very best way to come to their assistance is to take some advantage of interprovincial conferences or the occasions on which the representatives of the Department of Labour have to meet the representatives of labour in the provinces and discuss these matters with them in order to come to mutual understanding.
There is something else which strikes me. According to the British North America Act the federal parliament has exclusive jurisdiction in certain matters; the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction in others. Both of them are masters within their own bounds; they are not subject to interference from the other side. What has been said here-and I regret to be unable to agree with it-is that when the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction and this parliament has no jurisdiction at all;
when on the other hand this parliament has exclusive jurisdiction and the provinces have no jurisdiction at all, although according to our constitution neither has jurisdiction in the other field, when they meet together they say, "Well, there has been an agreement about it," and it is considered just as though they had concurrent jurisdiction.
Surely the Minister of Justice has had too much parliamentary experience to insist on this legislation any longer. In addition, after having read the summary of the report of the price spreads committee as it appeared in the press, I submit that this legislation would have to be changed in order to meet the recommendations contained in that report, if it is accepted. To me it is astounding that such a tree should grow from such a seed.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 5 inclusive agreed to.

In connection with this
section, a week or two ago a former president of the Weekly Newspapers' Association of Canada drew to my attention the fact that the weekly newspapers are the training ground for printers of all classes throughout our country, and he mentioned the fact that the apprentice starts in and must spend three or four years at the work before he becomes competent. It will be understood that an apprentice, who is employed for the same hours as the regular employee, really is not entitled to nor can he earn the same rate of pay. I should like to ask the minister if the subsection to which I referred meets the situation about which I was consulted.

THE CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES act, 1932
Mr. G. G. COOTE (Macleod) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 13, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Morand in the chair.
On section 1-Surrender of policy.

subtopic: SECOND READING
speechtext: I move that the word "six" be substituted for the word "five."

subtopic: SECOND READING
speechtext:
The present insurance act- does not set any maximum rate of interest which may be charged by a company on policy loans. The old act which was in force prior to 1932 provided for a maximum rate of seven per cent but when that act was amended in 1932 that particular section was left out. The companies are now free to charge any rate which may be stipulated. The rates charged on policy loans have varied all the way from five to ten per cent, according to a statement made in committee by the superintendent of insurance. Many companies have been charging seven per cent on their policy loans, while others have been chfc-ging six per cent. In a number of cases an extra charge of four per cent is made for loans automatically advanced under the non-forfeiture clause which appears in most of the policies issued by Canadian companies. This bill will not affect loans of this character. Counsel appearing for the Life Insurance Companies Association argued that the inclusion of a section of this kind would be unconstitutional. While I was not much impressed with that argument, I think the majority of the members of the committee were, and to avoid any possibility of this being considered unconstitutional, loans advanced under the non-forfeiture clause were not brought under the provisions of this bill.
In order that the members of the committee may realize the importance of this matter, I would point out that policy loans now outstanding in Canada amount to something like $250,000,000. A saving of even one per cent to the policyholders who have borrowed would amount to $2,500,000 per year. I think it would be just as well if I placed on record the amount of loans outstanding in the different years from 1926 to the present time. They were:
1923		 $ 81,316,648
1924		 90,208,571
1925		 98,780,875
1926		 108,550,314
1927		 119,735,561
1928		 133.697,625
1929		 159,353,195
1930		 188,723.474
1931		 218,579.939
1932		 244,163,978
I am sorry I have not the figures for the last two years, but I think the totals are slightly larger. As I said before, the loans outstanding at the present time are around $250,000,000. Loans of this kind are made on the best security which any life insurance company could have. The company cannot
Insurance Companies Act

possibly have a loss. There is no other form of investment open to companies to-day on which they can make six per cent, the rate asked for in the amendment moved by the hon. member. Last year, I believe, the largest life insurance company in Canada earned 4-08 per cent on their investment. That was the average rate. If that is all they can earn, why should the policyholder be charged a rate practically two per cent in excess of that? On dominion government bonds they cannot earn more than three per cent; and if you take into consideration the cost of administration, there is no other class of investment on which they can earn more than five per cent. Real estate mortgage is the only class of loans on which they can get a better rate than five per cent, and if you deduct the cost of operations you will find that to-day they cannot possibly get *5. return of even five per cent. I have here an article written by the assistant treasurer of Canada Life Insurance Company appearing in Canadian Insurance of February 12, in which he says that at the present time three per cent is about all the companies can earn on dominion government bonds. On British government bonds they can get a yield of approximately two and a half per cent, and on United States bonds less than three per cent. He goes on to say:
Insurance contracts require a certain definite rate of interest to be earned each year, in order that the policy reserves may be built up, which are necessary to make possible the payment of death claims and other policy payments as they fall due. In some companies, the rate of interest which must be earned to guarantee these benefits is three per cent, and in other companies it is three and one-half per cent.
I think that is clear proof that the company does not need a rate of interest in excess of three and a half per cent. When the banking committee, after considering the matter carefully, fixed the rate at five per cent, I certainly think the committee would be well advised to pass it at that rate or even lower. Certainly there is no justification for the members of this house allowing the insurance companies to charge policyholders a rate of six per cent.
One of the main reasons given against this bill in committee was that policyholders would borrow too much from the companies if the rate were reduced to five per cent. That argument is absolutely unsound and is not borne out by the facts. It was stated that if the rate was as low as that the policyholders would borrow against their policies in order to obtain money with which to specu-
late. Well, in the years when speculation was rife in Canada, from 1926 to 1929, policy loans increased, as I stated, from $108,000,000 in 1926 to $119,000,000 in 1927-not a large increase. They jumped to $188,000,000 in 1928, not a large increase, and in 1929 to $159,000,000. That was not a large increase either. In the deflation years which followed they quickly climbed up to $250,000,000. There was an increase in the amount borrowed by policyholders during the years from 1926 to 1930 of approximately, I should say, fifty per cent; but that does not at all correspond to the increase in the amount of insurance carried by the people of Canada during those years. That increased very much more rapidly than the loans which were taken out by policyholders.	.
The other argument advanced in the committee was that in a time of stress policyholders would borrow so much from the company, if the rate were as low as five per cent, that they would bankrupt the company; there would be such a run on the company that they could not find the funds. That is a preposterous idea. Only one-third of the policyholders of Canada are borrowers; the other two-thirds do not need to borrow, and if they did, I cannot possibly imagine that any life insurance company's manager would suppose that all the policyholders would want to borrow to the limit of their policies. But any money that any company has invested in a loan to a policyholder is, I submit, much safer than are a good many of the investments which the companies themselves made in the years 1927, 1928 and 1929. Anyone who reads the insurance bluebook will see many investments which are not worth more than fifty per cent of the money put into them. The money would be much safer invested in the form of loans to policyholders than invested, for instance, in a head office building in Montreal at a cost of over $20,000,000. It would be much safer than certain investments made by one of the largest life insurance companies operating in Canada and the United States, which has a mortgage of $27,000,000 on the Empire State building in New York and $56,000,000 on Radio City building, New York. Another one, through a mortgage, has become the owner of one of the largest night clubs.

I say to hon. members, however, that we have a duty to perform to policyholders who find themselves in the position of having to borrow to maintain their policies. The higher the rate of interest charged them on these loans, the sooner will their reserves be eaten up by interest on their loans.
One other argument which I may anticipate was advanced by some hon. members. It was stated that, only one-third of the policyholders being borrowers, by limiting the rate of interest to five per cent-the average is something over six per cent-it would be cutting down the profits of the policyholders who do not borrow. I do not think that is an ethical argument. Surely the policyholders who are not borrowers from the company should not want a profit at the expense of any policyholder who is only borrowing against an amount that is guaranteed to him as a loan value under his policy. If the insurance companies can earn only three per cent on high grade dominion government bonds, why should they want more than five per cent from a policyholder when he wishes to borrow a few dollars?
I hope it is not necessary to say anything more to this committee to convince them that when we set a maximum rate of five per cent interest to be charged by insurance companies against loans by policyholders, we are certainly being very liberal so far as the life insurance companies are concerned. Surely the companies exist for the benefit of the policyholders.

No, that is Canadian business. There is one other point I should mention, and that is that the life insurance companies control practically as large an amount of the savings of the Canadian people as do the chartered banks, and the rate of interest they charge is a determining factor in the general interest structure in this country. We cannot allow it to remain so high. One of the factors retarding the recovery of business in Canada is the high interest rates charged, and I submit that one of the best
things the committee can do is on every possible occasion to insist on lowering the interest rates. Here is one place where we have the right to interfere and to say that on loans to policyholders the maximum rate of interest should not be more than five per cent. I think, as I said a moment ago, we are very liberal to the insurance companies when we fix the rate of interest at five per cent. A good many members have expressed to me the opinion that the rate should be four per cent. I did introduce the bill with a four per cent rate, but I judged from the discussion which took place in the committee that perhaps I would be wise to accept a compromise on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Pettit) which sought to fix the rate at five per cent. I hope this committee will see fit to reject the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White), and to pass the bill providing for a rate of five per cent.

subtopic: SECOND READING
speechtext: I am heartily in support of the mover of this bill and against the amendment to make the rate [DOT] six per cent. I take this attitude, because I feel the high rate of interest that has prevailed particularly in the western parts of Canada is one of the main causes of the difficulty in which many of our people find themselves; a good deal of the distress is due to the fact that they have had to pay such high rates of interest. Of course I can understand that on a farm mortgage there is a certain amount of risk, and probably for that reason there is some justification for the rates being a little higher than on other types of loans. But in such a case as this where a man is really only borrowing back a part of his own money, it seems to me that the insurance company will take precautions not to allow him to borrow enough to introduce any very great risk. I think, as the sponsor of the bill has said, we are very generous to the life insurance companies in allowing them to charge five per cent. I would have supported him even had the rate been left at four per cent, for the simple reason that there is very little, if any, risk in connection with loans made under these conditions. I am not going to delay the committee any longer except to say that I heartily support the bill providing for a rate of five per cent, and I will oppose the amendment that has been moved in connection therewith.

subtopic: SECOND READING
speechtext:
The general rate of
interest in the Dominion of Canada for the past four or five years has in my opinion been quite out of line with everything else; interest
Insurance Companies Act

rates have been absolutely too high. I remember back in 1928 and 1929, when we in the west were getting 81.60 a bushel for our wheat, we were paying seven and even eight per cent interest for money, but to-day when we are getting somewhere in the neighbourhood of sixty cents a bushel for our wheat, we are still paying these high rates of interest.
The same thing applies to wages. Back in 1928 and 1929 I was paying from $5 to $7 a day for a man to work in the harvest field and paying seven or eight per cent interest for money. To-day a man cannot get a job in a harvest field for SI a day, but we are still paying the same high rates of interest. The price of labour and the price of commodities have come down, but that for money has not, and it is time it should be lowered so as to be somewhat on a parity with the price of everything else.
I am well aware that in order to reduce rates of interest we must begin with our main securities such as our federal, provincial and municipal bonds, and lower the rates on them. After we do that we shall have the rates on mortgages and on private loans from banks and other corporations come down in proportion. But a loan from an insurance company is the best risk there is in the country; there is no other loan that is as secure as that lent by an insurance company. It is really lending a man his own money; in every case a man has paid his money into the insurance company, and when he finds himself in difficulties he asks it to lend him a little of his own money. The insurance company is in no danger whatever of losing that money. Such a loan is better than federal, provincial or any other kind of bonds, and the rate charged by insurance companies should be in some way comparable with rates on federal and provincial bonds. Some will say:	If you begin
to allow a man to borrow on his insurance he will use the insurance companies instead of the banks. Well, people did not do this years ago in western Canada. At that time money could be borrowed from life insurance companies at six per cent, but although we were paying seven, eight, nine and even as high as ten per cent interest for money, we continued to borrow from the banks and did not go to our insurance companies for loans. Why then should we fear that the insurance companies will be used as lending concerns? There is no danger of that. A man does not borrow money on his insurance unless he is having very hard times and is right up against it. The only time he borrows money from insurance companies is when he needs the money in the worst possible way.

I am heartily in agreement with this bill. I say that the rate of interest should be even, lower than five per cent; it should be reduced to four per cent so that it may be in some way comparable with the rate of interest on federal bonds. Formerly the rate on loans by insurance companies was six per cent, but there is a service charge on top of that. Many of the companies were charging six per cent and two per cent in addition for service. One of the biggest insurance companies in the dominion was charging six per cent for the loan and two per cent for service; some were charging as high as four per cent for service, making the rate of interest ten per cent. This is outrageous and it is time that this practice should be checked. We have to begin somewhere to reduce the rate of interest. In the banking and commerce committee two years ago we discussed the whole debt structure of the dominion. Where did we get? We got nowhere; we did nothing; we came back to the house, and all we had was some nice literature describing the financial condition of the provinces and the dominion. But we did not do anything, and it is high time that a beginning was made somewhere. We might as well begin with our main, first class securities, such as insurance loans where we are borrowing money on our life insurance to tide us over times of difficulty and distress. If we cannot borrow that at a lower rate of interest, it is time we should, and I am heartily in agreement with the reduction in the rate to five per cent and even lower.
