As mover of the amendment, Mr. Chairman, I desire to say a word or two. The suggestion of the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) that all loans on life insurance policies should be prohibited is novel, but it has no relation to the bill under discussion. There is this point to be considered, however, that if loans on policies should be totally prohibited except in respect of what I understand are called automatic loans, the result would be the expiration of the policies and the beneficiaries, whom the hon. member would safeguard, would not derive any benefit whatsoever.
I regret that I cannot share the view, certainly not in its entirety, expressed by the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens). I agree with him that one of the most serious deterrents to the recovery of business in Canada to-day, possibly, is not the heavy weight of interest so much as the heavy weight of debt and the taxation that arises therefrom. The public have not very much control over the matter of debt; what we call the power of the people in respect of government is somewhat illusory. Our debt has been created, in the main, through the great war, over which the people of Canada certainly had no control. It has been created in no small part through railway policies which are now generally admitted to have been misconceived, and the weight of taxation consequent upon this debt presses upon business seriously whether the rate of commercial or other loans be three per cent, four per cent, five per cent, or six per cent.
I should like to point out that loans made by insurance companies on policies in past years have borne interest, as has been stated, as high as ten per cent, which I agree is an
extremely high rate. The nominal rate was six or seven per cent, and upon that nominal rate was piled a service charge of two and three and I am told, even four per cent. It appeared from the evidence before the banking and commerce committee that at present the rate of interest on loans upon policies is about eight per cent. It is now proposed by the amendment which I have moved, to reduce that rate to six per cent. That is a cut of twenty-five per cent-no mean reduction-and it will to that extent relieve those who borrow upon policies.
However, to my mind this is the very strongest argument that can be put forward against the reduction in the rate of interest or against even a six per cent rate, namely, that the insurance companies do not cultivate this type of business. It is true that as an inducement to prospective policyholders a clause is inserted in the policy to the effect that after a certain period, when sufficient premiums have been paid to give a stated value to the policy, a loan may be obtained upon it. That may be, I presume it is, an excellent selling point, but the companies do not cultivate this class of business at all, and when the companies are not wanting that class of business I submit that it is a fair deduction to say that it is not a desirable business for the companies.
An impressive argument upon the other side is that the insurance companies net from their investments to-day a figure somewhere in the neighbourhood of three and a half per cent, therefore, say those who would fix the rate at four per cent, why charge the poor policyholder who wants a loan six per cent or even five per cent? But the difference is this: When the companies invest in a dominion bond, a provincial or a municipal government bond, they know that they have an asset in their strong box which is good over a long term of years, and which costs them not a penny to administer beyond the wear and tear on the scissors which cut the coupons, whereas when they make a loan on a policy there is annually, and I dare say in most cases semi-annually, a certain amount of clerical work to be done and a certain expenditure imposed upon the company in connection with that loan, which expenditure reduces very substantially the net amount received from the loan.
I said a moment ago that the service charge is two per cent. If we make the rate six per cent now without a service charge, that makes it equivalent to a rate of four per cent. Is that not clear? Is that not logical? Is that not so? There are some $250,000,000 of loans outstanding upon the
Copyright Act

insurance policies of the Canadian companies, a figure which represents I think about thirty per cent of the total amount of insurance in force with these companies. Now my interest in this whole question is that of a policyholder, and no other whatsoever. I have only the interest of a policyholder. I am one of the other seventy per cent of the insurance policyholders in this country. The gentleman who wants a five per cent rate, and would prefer a four per cent rate, represents only thirty per cent of the policyholders of this country. I object to a lower rate than six per cent because under that rate the companies will have a stronger financial structure and will be upon a surer foundation, and I as one of seventy per cent of the policyholders have in mind first and last only the interest and solvency of the insurance companies.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext:
The house proceeded to the consideration of the amendments made by the senate to Bill No. 15-Mr. Rhodes-to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act.
I Mr. R. S. White.]

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendments made by the Senate to this bill will be found in votes and proceedings of yesterday. In addition they have been incorporated1 in the bill itself, which has been circulated and I believe is now either on the file or in the post office box of every hon. member. I do not propose to go into the details of the various amendments, which are numerous, but I shall refer to one or two.
It will be recalled that- in the bill passed by this house it was provided that the maximum amount of a loan upon first mortgage would be $7,500. The Senate has reduced this figure to $5,000. In connection with the combination of first and second mortgages plus the added security provided1 in the bill, the maximum amount in the bill as it left this house was $7,500, but the Senate has reduced this to $6,000. No doubt there will be a difference of opinion as to which is preferable, but I understand that the argument which resulted in this amendment was to the effect that to the extent the amount of individual loans was reduced, there would be an increase in the amount available and in the number who would have an opportunity of participating in the total amount whidh the board would have to pay out by way of loans. In the circumstances I am prepared to concur in that amendment.
However there is one amendment made by the Senate to which I take exception. The bill as it left this house provided that the maximum amount which could be lent upon a combination of the real estate, the buildings and the collateral security by way of chattel mortgage would be sixty-six and two-thirds per cent of the appraised value in every province save Quebec. In Quebec where they have no chattel1 mortgages the figure was to by sixty per cent. The Senate amendments provide that the maximum amount of loan in the first case would be sixty per cent and in the province of Quebec, fifty-five per cent. My main reason for taking exception to these amendments is that we have the right to assume, I think, that farm property at the present time is about at its lowest value. If a farmer should secure a total advance of sixty six and two-thirds per cent of a fair appraisal of the value of his farm he would in effect be securing a much smaller loan than he would have secured under a fifty per cent valuation a few years ago. For that reason, if for none other, we feel that we should adhere to the larger percentages.
After all is said and done, much will depend upon the valuation. It would take a very skilful valuator to value a property within six and two-thirds per cent. I have the feel-

Farm Loan Act
ing with respect to the larger figure that there will be an opportunity presented to the deserving farmer who is a good moral risk. He will be more apt to obtain his loan with the larger figure than he would if the valuator were faced with the difficulty of appraising the value of a farm at a sufficient figure to enable a loan to be advanced. Without labouring the matter any further, I move, seconded by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Sutherland):
That all the amendments proposed by the Senate to Bill No. 15, an act to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act, be concurred in, with the exception of amendments Nos. 13 and 14, in which amendments this house does not concur for the following reason: That farm property being at the present time at its lowest value, a total advance of sixty-six and two-thirds per cent of the appraised value of a farm would secure a much smaller loan than would' have been secured at fifty per cent valuation a few years ago.
I hope I have made it clear that my motion provides for the acceptance of all the amendments with the exception of the two noted.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I would submit to the Minister of Finance that these amendments appeared only yesterday in the votes and proceedings. They are extensive and in many cases very important, and I suggest to the minister that further consideration be permitted until Monday. While I agree with the two exceptions which the minister has made in his general acceptance, I believe there should be other exceptions included in his motion. I disagree with the action of the Senate in reducing the total amount of loan on the land and buildings to $5,000. In the original bill the amount provided was $10,000. Last year's amendments provided for a reduction to $7,500, and now the Senate has proposed a further reduction to $5,000. That is going a little too far. Next, they have stricken out the option of the borrower with regard to the amortization principle in connection with the repayment of the loan. That in itself may not be of extreme importance but it did have some merit in so far as certain borrowers were concerned.
I am at a loss to understand fully all that is meant in the substitution for the original subsection (h) of section 7 of the proposal now made in the senate amendments. It reads:
(h) Except as provided in, and subject to, such regulations, not inconsistent with the provisions of the Interest Act, as the board may prescribe, any borrower may at any time repay the whole or part of his loan on any date on which an instalment becomes due.
When the payment is part of the loan only it shall be credited to the borrower in such manner as the board may by regulation prescribe, but so that no such payment shall relieve the borrower from liability to pay or from continuing to pay, at the times agreed upon, the various instalments next ensuing due after such partial payment is made, and until the loan and interest is repaid in full.
My reading of that clause would lead me to believe that it would mean that any prepayment of any portion of the amount due would apply at the end of the loan and not to subsequently ensuing payments of the loan. I believe that this again should be at the option of the borrower; he should have the right to say, "I may want this amount applied on my next payment." Take the farmer who has an exceptionally favourable crop or who has touched an exceptionally favourable market: he may want, as a matter of precaution against possible ensuing failures, to apply the amount on the loan either on next ensuing payments or on payments beyond that. But this clause would appear to give power to the board to determine that the payment shall apply at the expiry of the mortgage and not at any time designated by the borrower.
I object also to the amendment proposed in subsection (j) of section 7. The new subsection (j) reads:
It shall be a term of any mortgage taken as security for a loan that upon the sale or lease of the farm land mortgaged the loan shall, at the option of the board, immediately become due and payable.
The Senate has included the words "or lease," which now makes it imperative on the man to recognize that the board may compel him to accept the mortgage as having matured in the event of his leasing the land. Someone says, Why not? For this reason- that in many instances a farmer, during the term of the loan, becomes incapable through illness or because of age of carrying on as the actual operator and occupant of the farm. His loan may still have a period to run, and yet this clause would give power to the board to compel him to meet the full obligation under the loan at that time, and his property would become subject to the board. That is extremely unfair. So far as I can ascertain, the farm loan act loses its value to those who want to borrow under it-those, for example, who have become aged, those who have become ill during the occupancy of the farm, and, of course, members of parliament who find it difficult to carry on both occupations. No member who leases his farm is in a position to secure a loan under the act
Farm Loan Act

because, if he is not in occupancy of the farm, he does not get a loan.
I take gravest exception to the amendments to section 8 of the act. Subsection 3 of the new provisions, and indeed all the new provisions-and by the way they cover nearly two pages of the votes and proceedings-are directed to the strange purpose of removing from under the provinces all lands in connection with which money is borrowed from the board. They remove from the jurisdiction of all provincial legislatures, with respect to lands, anyone who borrows money from the board. That was not done under the old act. It is an entirely new conception on the part of the Senate; and to make it perfectly clear that this was their purpose, it is provided that such moneys as may be due, such lands as may be hypothecated, shall be regarded as the land or property or money of His Majesty the King in the right of the Dominion of Canada. Subsection 3, however, removes any difficulty in understanding the purpose of the Senate with respect to these amendments. It reads:
(3) Notwithstanding any law, -whether statute or other, now in force or which hereafter may be in force in any province, no mechanics' lien law, taxation lien law or other law or privilege of any species whatever where-under liens, charges or privileges upon or against land or other property of any species whatever erected, arise or exist shall, without the consent in writing of the board, which consent shall be revocable, affect or apply to any land or other property of any species whatever or any part thereof or interest therein, to which any mortgage or other security, lien, charge or privilege made or given to the board under this act after the thirtieth day of June, 1935, shall relate, in prejudice of the board as the holder of any such mortgage or other security, lien, charge or privilege so made or given, but every such mortgage or other security, lien, charge or privilege thereafter made or given to the board shall, for so long as it shall remain wholly or partially unpaid, rank upon such land or other property or part thereof or interest therein, as the case may be, in priority to all other securities, liens, charges or privileges, whatsoever.
It shall rank in priority to school taxes and to all .other taxes; and indeed anyone who borrows under this act may lose any privilege or protection he now has under any debt adjustment law of any province. This was never intended by this house. When the House of Commons accepted the farm loan act some years ago and the amendments of last year as well as those of this year, there was never, in my opinion, the thought in the mind of any member that the borrower under the act should lose any of his rights or privileges under provincial laws in respect of chattel mortgages, farm mortgages or land

hens. The Senate has taken away from the borrower any privilege or right he has to-day under the lien laws of the respective provinces. These are my chief objections to the amendments provided by the Senate; but the whole thing is so involved, the terminology is so complex and legal that the average lay member must have great difficulty in understanding it after the brief opportunity we have had for its perusal. I suggest therefore that the minister might allow the matter to stand over until Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I am not entitled to speak at this stage, but I would ask unanimous consent to do so, not to reply to my hon. friend, as I should like to, but to indicate my appreciation of his difficulty. I spent as much time as I could spare from my other work this morning going through the various amendments and I could demonstrate that the hon. gentleman's fears with respect to them are unfounded. As a matter of fact the amendment to which he. took greatest exception was designed solely for the benefit and protection of the borrower. My concern, however, is to get the bill back to the Senate and to have it become law. So far as I am personally concerned I should be happy to facilitate my hon. friend from Bow River. But assuming that his argument were sound, it would be far better to have the bill completed, even if not altogether satisfactory in terms, have royal assent given to it next week and have the money made available to the farmers than, by delaying it until Monday with an adjournment coming on Wednesday, to come to the point where we may have to adjourn without this bill passing, thus denying the farmers of this country over a period of the year when they need loans more than at any other time, an opportunity to secure them. I had that in mind in reducing my opposition to the Senate amendments in the hope that the Senate might concur so as to enable the bill to pass there and receive royal assent on Wednesday.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I do not think we would be delaying the bill by letting it stand over until Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I have no objection.

speechtext: -for the simple reason that the Senate will not meet until Tuesday, and if we dispose of the bill on Monday they will be in a position to take it up in the Senate on Tuesday in any case. If the minister cannot answer that now, possibly between to-night and Monday he might give it consideration and be able to tell us on Monday when the bill will be in operation.

courtesy of the chair and the house. I apologize to the house for craving its indulgence for just one moment. There appears in to-night's newspapers a Canadian Press dispatch, and I am reading from page 21 of the five o'clock edition of the Ottawa Journal these words:
After his resignation, Mr. Stevens said, the Prime Minister divulged' to the public details of privy council discussions which is contrary, he claimed, to the oath of office.
I cannot conceive how anyone could have placed such words in my mouth. The nearest approach to them that I find in the Hansard report of my remarks is this:
I resigned for that purpose and for that reason, that the secret and private discussions of cabinet had been spread upon the pages of the press.
I wish to thank the house for this opportunity of making that brief denial or correction, because of the significance of the words which were wrongfully published.
12, 1935	2701
________Supply-Agriculture-Farms

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Bury in the chair.
Experimental farms, including investigations concerning plant diseases, $1,937,898.

Has the
minister given any further consideration to the suggestion that has been made so often in the house that one of these experimental farms should be put on an ordinary operating basis and that the minister should provide the house from time to time with information as to the possibility or otherwise of attempting to carry on an experimental farm under ordinary conditions? This suggestion, which as I recall it was made many years ago, would, if carried out, prove of immense value as a fair test of whether agriculture, at least in certain sections of the country, could be regarded as a profitable profession. It would certainly be a better means of informing governments of actual conditions than the varying reports on costs and so forth that come from all parts of the country. Has the minister given any consideration to this?

I agree entirely with the hon. member for Bow River that it is very important as far as we are able to get accurate costs of production. It is the purpose on at least one farm, or possibly more than one, to carry out, in a little different way from what has formerly been the case, a scheme based on costs of production. But even in that case the hon. member will realize that there will be overhead expenses like those of a superintendent of the farm and perhaps a clerk to keep accurate costs. On such a farm, however, we shall be able to get accurate information as to the profit or lack of it in farming in the locality in which the farm is situated. At the same time surveys are being conducted of the costs of operation of farms in different localities throughout the country. But I agree with the hon. member that it is desirable so far as possible to get the most accurate information as to the cost of farming using the methods I believe the hon. member has in mind, advocated by the experimental farm system.

Has any
experimental work in that connection been so far undertaken?

Supply-Agriculture-Farms

It is the intention
to undertake work of that kind in the new farm that we set up at Melfort, to make it as nearly as possible a farm operated by a fanner.
Nothing has yet been done?
Nothing except surveys of individual farms.

Can the minister give the committee any accurate figures on production costs based on the results so far secured in connection with the individual test farms that he is speaking about? Eor instance, can he give the cost of wheat?

Illustration station cost figures are published annually. There are several reports that deal with that. In addition, the head of the farm management department in the university of Saskatchewan, Professor Allen, has devoted a great deal of time to that, but I have not his report under my hand at the moment.
He is doing it for the university?
Yes, it is outside the illustration farm system.

Yes, I have known for some years of Doctor Allen's work; it probably is the outstanding example of the thing we are trying to get. What he is doing is surveying conditions as they are to-day and basing conclusions on that. I believe he is now undertaking similar work for Alberta. But I was speaking of the type of farms to which the minister referred a minute ago.
Our work has to do with illustration stations and also the economic survey.

Last year on the public works program passed towards the end of the session the Minister of Agriculture promised me that some of that money would be spent on the experimental farm at Kapuskasmg. I gave him then certain facts of which I had personal knowledge, because I visit that farm every year; I knew of certain improvements that were necessary to* buildings. We are thankful that some of the money was spent there, but having made further personal inspection I would again ask the minister if he can find it possible to proceed a little further with such improvements. The experimental farm at Kapuskasing is a great asset to that section and is very well administered. Every

section of our population would highly appreciate the continuation of the work that was started there last year under the public works program. Will the minister give me an answer the same as last year?
Yes.

The Swift Current experimental farm has been without a superintendent for some considerable time, I believe since last June. Would the minister care to tell the committee what the plan is in connection with that farm, particularly in regard to the policy that is to be pursued? The Swift Current farm has been working along the lines of dry farming, with special reference to the needs of the open prairie section. Is there to be a continuation of that policy, or what is the attitude of the department towards the Swift Current farm?

The delay in the appointment of a superintendent has been occasioned to a certain extent by a stepping up of the grade of the superintendent The man we hope to make superintendent will have the supervision not only of the Swift Current station but also of other works connected with it, that is range work and so on. The matter is now in the hands of the civil service commission. The position has been advertised and applications are being received, and as soon as the time expires an appointment will be made.
It is not contemplated to make any change in the policy that has been pursued there for a number of years?
No, just to widen it and connect it up with the range work.
I take it that the increase in this item is due to the launching of the new farm at Melfort?

No, it is due to a
number of causes.

Could the
minister give the details of the increase?

It is spread over
a wide range-increased grant for fruit investigations, for range investigations, particularly in British Columbia; soil surveys will be extended; black soil investigations in the east; general equipment for laboratories, and increased building equipment.

What is
the total amount required for the new farm?

$25,000.

Supply-Agriculture-Farms
Where did the minister say it was-?
Melfort.
Has the minister the information before him as to the cost of the farm at Agassiz, how many persons are employed, and the number of persons that visit that farm?

The appropriation
is $37,000. There is a classified staff of five. We have not a record here of the number of visitors, but as the hon. member knows it is one of the farms that perhaps has the greatest number of visitors.

I made a suggestion last year
-I do not know whether the minister ever looked into it-as to the advisability of moving that farm into the Chilliwack district, where it would be of far more advantage than it is in its present location. An experimental farm is of no use unless it is accessible to the people. This farm was established in the early days of settlement, and now the population is all on the other side of the river, so that if the farm were moved there the people could easily inspect it and thereby get some advantage from it.

May I ask the minister
if there is a butter factory at the central experimental farm?

Just for making
home butter.

As experiments in butter
making are carried on in most experimental farms, it would be in order to refer to a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture on Friday last about our dairy trade with Great Britain. I will tell the minister exactly what happened. Referring to a previous debate, the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Parent) said to the minister-I have this distinctly in mind; I have it upstairs in print and could get it in a moment- that the minister had declared that the United Kingdom was the best market for dairy products. The minister replied, " I did not say that." Now, without using anew the word " that," may I ask what the minister meant by such a reply. I stated the case to him very clearly last Friday, as recorded at page 2497 of Hansard. Now I have Hansard of last year, and at page 1590 it reads:
Mr. Weir (Melfort): Did the hon. member say I stated this afternoon that the United Kingdom was the best market for our dairy-produce?
Mr. Parent: I understood the minister to say that.
Mr. Weir (Melfort): I did' not say it.
Mr. Parent: I accept the minister's statement.
Mr. Pouliot: Therefore the Ottawa agreements are of no use.
May I ask the hon. gentleman what he meant when he declared that he had not said the words mentioned by the hon. member for Terrebonne?

Mr. Chairman, this subject would I believe rightly come under the second next item that we are going to take, namely, cold storage and dairying, and in case further information should be asked for, I will ask that the matter referred to by the hon. member for Temiscouata be left until that item is under discussion. But since the hon. member has asked the question, and to make it clear that there is no desire to evade answering, I would say that what I said I do not think could be put in simpler language-that I did not say in the statement I made that the United Kingdom was the best market. It might be considered the best market; it might be the best market, but the point I made was that I did not make that statement, and the hon. member for Terrebonne accepted my statement in that connection. That deals only with the fact that I said I did not make the statement the hon. member suggested I had made; there was no controversy other than that.

But there is a reason for everything, and I am going to ask one more question of the minister; after that he will be through with me at least so far as this item is concerned. Why did he say he had not made the statement?
Because I had not made it. [DOT]

This is quite amusing,
but it is not illuminating. If the matter was of no importance I do not see why a minister of the crown should say he never made the statement. When a minister says he did not make a previous declaration it is because that declaration is of great importance. When the minister is himself he is most agreeable to deal with; when he spoke in that way he was true to himself and he did not want to give the Canadian public the impression that the United Kingdom was our best market for Canadian dairy products. I may be wrong but it is my humble view that when that statement was imputed to the minister by the hon. member for Terrebonne, the minister knew that Canadian butter had been shipped back tu

Supply-Agriculture-Farms
Canada after having been in the United Kingdom for some time, and found it impossible to let it go like that when the hon. member for Terrebonne mentioned that statement. I am sure the minister realized that the United Kingdom is not our best .market for dairy products, and that was why he rose in reply to the hon. member for Terrebonne and denied the statement that had been imputed to him.

If the debate is
resolving itself into a question whether I know why I gave the answer or whether the hon. member knows, I do not think anything is to be gained by prolonging the discussion. I was only keeping the hon. member for Terrebonne, who was very sincere in his discussion, straight so far as a statement I made was concerned. If the hon. member for Terrebonne had wished to find out what in my opinion, which after all is only my opinion as an individual, is the best market for our butter, he would have asked me that direct question and I would have given him my opinion. It was because I thought he had misunderstood something I had said that I stated I had not made that statement, without any attempt to evade giving information. There is nothing to be gained in attempting to do that, because all infoma-tion has to be brought forward and it is our desire to do so. So far as our butter is concerned I think it is generally admitted that our home market is the best market; that is why we have given protection to our own farmers. So far as my answer to the hon. member for Terrebonne is concerned certainly there was no evasion; it was simply a desire on my part to make certain that he was not making his statement feeling that I had said something I had not said.

I am not a mind reader, of course, though the minister said at first I had answered for him. I need not insist further; I thank the minister for his very frank statement to the effect that our home market is our best market for dairy products.
I said for butter.

Very well, for butter. I will not speak of cheese or other dairy products; the facts and figures are on record. According to the statement just made by the Minister of Agriculture our home market is the best market for butter; it is better than the British market. I am satisfied with that answer, and there is only one thing I regret. It is that at present the price of butter in the United States is much higher than it is in Canada, so much so that butter has to be

smuggled from Canada to the United States. I regret also that in Canada there is a smaller consumption of farm products, some of which are grown and advertised by our experimental farms. We have no local market as it was in previous days; the farmer has lost even his home market, and I regret it, though the minister says our home market is the best market for butter.

I should like to direct a few questions to the minister, and first I should like to ask him something about the Rosthem farm and the Seager Wheeler property. I would like the minister to tell me also who is the superintendent of that farm at the present time and what in particular is being done at the Rosthern farm and the Seager Wheeler property.

Mr. Hutton is the officer in charge of the Rosthern experimental farm. The work that is being carried on there is in connection with dairying and live stock, especially pigs, and one of the chief projects carried on there is horticulture. On Seager Wheeler's farm the work is of a demonstrative nature in grains, in plant breeding, of cereals and horticultural plants. We have the use of Doctor Wheeler's farm, his own time and the labour on the farm for, I think $2,100 a year.
If the minister has it I wonder if he could give a comparative statement as to the cost of operating the different experimental farms.
I have the estimates for this year. Does the hon. member want them for all the farms throughout Canada?
The hon. member for Macdonald tells me that a return giving this information has been brought down and is available.
I thought I brought it down.

The hon. member says it has been brought down, so the minister need not answer that question; I can find the information elsewhere. Something has been said about the new farm about to be set up, if not already in operation, at Melfort. For the information of the committee would the minister tell us the distance in miles between the Rosthem experimental farm and the proposed new farm at Melfort? I understand that is the closest farm to the new farm.

Supply-Agriculture-Farms

I have not the mileage here, but if my memory serves me aright it is eighty or eighty-five miles from Rosthern to my own farm and about thirty-five miles from there to Melfort, but by direct road the distance would be somewhat less than that. I assume the hon. member is trying to get at why a farm should be placed as close, comparatively, to the Rosthern farm as it is proposed that the Melfort farm should be. It is not as close to the Rosthern farm as the farm at Saskatoon. It is about the same distance as the Scott experimental farm. But it is not a question of miles. It is because there is no experimental farm situated on soil typical of that at Melfort, and that is typical of the greater part of the soil all the way from Dauphin to the Alberta boundary. In order that hon. members may realize the extent of that very large area I may say that the Carrot river valley is situated practically in the centre of that whole area, and it is the largest area of cultivated soil that is in a reasonably close compass. The Melfort farm is situated pretty much in the centre of that area, and in order that hon. members may have some idea of the extent and production of that area in the. Carrot river valley alone I think it advisable that I should put this information on Hansard.
The area under cultivation in the Carrot river valley is 1,130,825 acres, almost three times the area of the cultivated land in British Columbia, and greater than the total area of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. The production in this area in 1931, the census year which gives us the most accurate figures, was as follows: Melfort produced 10,927,916 bushels of wheat, while Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and British Columbia combined produced only 2,898,000 bushels of wheat; that is, in the Carrot river valley approximately four times as much was produced as in all these other provinces combined.
There was also produced in that area one and a half times as much barley as was produced in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, and British Columbia combined, the Carrot river valley producing 5,303,584 bushels of barley while these other provinces combined produced only
3,350,000	bushels. The Carrot river valley produced almost thirty-seven per cent of the barley produced in Saskatchewan; it produced almost eight per cent of all the barley produced in the Dominion of Canada. It produced 25-5 per cent as much barley as Alberta; it produced 34-4 per cent as much barley as
Manitoba, and 39-3 per cent as much barley as Ontario produced. In 1931 the Carrot river valley produced almost one-thirtieth of the total wheat produced in Canada; more than one-twelfth of the wheat produced in Saskatchewan; almost one-thirteenth as much wheat as Alberta produced, and over one-third as much wheat as the whole of Manitoba produced.
In 1932 there was marketed in the Carrot river valley one out of every seven hogs marketed in Saskatchewan, and more than one out of every forty-five hogs marketed in Canada.
I think I heard one hon. member suggest that when we were having such excellent results there why was it necessary to put in an experimental farm? The reason is I think self-evident. That large area to the north, because of the high price of wheat, went almost entirely into the production of wheat, although later it went into the production of some of the coarse grains. We believe that that whole belt of country from Dauphin to Alberta is particularly suited for mixed farming-not just wheat alone; there must be experiments made somewhere in that area, and it was natural that that district should have been decided upon as the largest cultivated district to give leadership to the farmers there who wished to change their methods of farming.
The population of the Carrot river valley is perhaps the most cosmopolitan of any similar district in the dominion. There are large numbers of settlers there from Scandinavian countries. For eight miles west of my own farm on both sides of the road every farmer is Scandinavian by race, and for six miles east all but three are of that same race. There is also a very large settlement of French-speaking people from the province of Quebec and some from the old land. We have as well settlers from every province in the dominion. This is I think the best compliment that I can pay them as farmers:	In

I wish to submit a certain number of questions to the minister and in doing so I point out to him what I and others in the maritime provinces regard as an injustice to growers of potatoes at least in New Brunswick, and I think the same situation applies to the other two maritime provinces. For instance I find in the price list issued by the board, prices fixed for export, Halifax. $1.50 per barrel, and 65 cents per bag of 90 pounds. But there is no price fixed for export from the port of Saint John. I should like to know why an export price is fixed only from the port of Halifax. 1 do not expect the minister to be able to give me an answer to-night to the various questions that I am going to submit; ha will find them in Hansard to-morrow and I would ask that he look carefully into them and the objections I am going to place on Hansard in regard to this organization, the eastern potato marketing scheme. Having stated this export price at Halifax and pointed out that no price is fixed at Saint John, I want to know if this means that potatoes for export can be shipped only through the port of Halifax. Then in the instructions issued I find that car lot shipments within Canada must have a government inspector's certificate attached to the car. I have no objection to that, but I also find the following in the instructions:
The buyer shall be entitled to inspection at destination, and this privilege shall be so marked on the bill of lading.
The inspection at point of shipment is made by government officials. I understand a fee of S3 is charged for that. I have no objection to a second inspection at point of destination provided that inspection is made by a government official. But as I understand the working of the scheme, that inspection of potatoes from New Brunswick at Montreal, for instance, is made by the purchaser, not by a government official. Now what will happen and what is happening if that is the case? If the purchaser is allowed to disregard the government inspection at
[Mr. R. Weird
point of shipment and base his price in Montreal on his own inspection, it becomes a monopoly for the dealer. He can turn down the potatoes. It is provided under the law that he shall have that- right of inspection, and if he is so minded, if he. is not one of the most honest men in the world, he can say:	"I had these potatoes inspected;
they do not come up to the mark, therefore I will not pay the price agreed upon," which is a price fixed' by the marketing board as a minimum price on the rails at Montreal. I am taking Montreal as an example. I want to know, and our shippers in New Brunswick want to know, why this second inspection is allowed without strict government supervision.
Then in the fixing of prices I find that the price is fixed only as at point of destination. If it is reasonable and right to fix the minimum price at point of destination, say Montreal or Toronto, why is it not right to fix a minimum price for the grower? Today the price is fixed at Montreal, I think at 55 cents or thereabouts for a bag of 90 pounds. Added to that must be the freight and the inspection fee, and the fee, I think it is called1, that is collected by the board to meet certain expenses. Then the price fixed, with these additions, plus the wholesale dealer's profit, is the price to the retail trade.
Since I am dealing with the retail trade at points of destination, how is it that the local marketing board so-called in Toronto can fix a minimum price to the retail trade? What right have they to fix such minimum price? We talk of ethics in business; we have had investigations before the price spreads commission of unethical methods of dealing with sales and purchases. How is it that the local board1-I have it here under date of March 17-can fix a price at Toronto for No. 1 potatoes of 83 cents per 90-pound bag for retail for Ontario potatoes and on potatoes from Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick at $1.09 a bag for the same weight? Then this board has entered into an agreement with certain chain stores that they shall keep the retail price of Ontario potatoes at such a figure as to debar the sale of potatoes from the east. If this can go on under this marketing scheme it is readily seen how injurious will be the effect upon the potato growers of eastern Canada. If Ontario as a whole cannot supply the demand in the Toronto market they have to import, but until the Ontario crop is disposed of this semi-monopoly is maintained, detrimental to the interests of potato growers in the east.

Under grade 1 there are four classifications, I think, for potatoes to be sold in the province of Ontario and the provinces east of Ontario, which would include Quebec and the maritime provinces. Under grade 2 you find potatoes graded for export, and this is different from the grade for sale in the provinces I have mentioned. A few weeks ago I asked a question in order to ascertain how many meetings had been held in the province of New Brunswick to explain this new marketing scheme to the potato producers. The minister gave me the number; I think it was eighteen or more, but it does not make very much difference. I have attempted to discover how these meetings were called. Last October or November there was a meeting called in my own county, about sixteen miles from my home. It could not have been very well advertised, because I knew nothing about it and heard nothing about it. I should like to have heard of it; I should like to have attended that meeting. I found that the gentleman who is head of the affair in the northern counties held a meeting at Belkdune, Gloucester county; another at Charlo Station, in Restigouche county, and another meeting at Balmoral, Restigouche county. At those meetings he told the people that the system of grading that was to be introduced would not affect the grading as it was carried on in New Brunswick in the past. What do we find? Those people have been deceived; the grading done to-day in New Brunswick is entirely different from the grading that was done previously under an act of parliament. They were told that there would be no difference, but the difference has been so great that in many places the farmers are unable to grade their potatoes for sale to dealers who buy them for resale, because under the regulations issued under the act and under this scheme when the farmer sells his potatoes to a dealer for resale those potatoes must be graded, and if he has not graded them he is liable to a fine of from $25 to $500, or to imprisonment. Under these rules the grading must be done by using expensive racking machines. In some parts of the province of New Brunswick I have no doubt that can be done to advantage. In the counties along the river St. John, in Carleton county, in Victoria, in Madawaska and in those counties bordering on the state of Maine, they can afford to do that, because they produce veiy large quantities of potatoes. But in other parts of the province, in northern New Brunswick, where the farmer produces for sale only say 150 to

My information is that there are constant violations of the regulations under this system of trucking. Not that I wish to argue that the transportation by truck of the farmers' produce should be done away with, but rather that the regulations governing the transportation of potatoes within a province or without a province should be observed. If they are not, what is the use of them? There is no use in having regulations at all if they are not observed, and the violation of these regulations does a great injustice to the producers of potatoes in other parts of Canada.
